da-9-1.answer:
Baseline circulating T cell populations that associate with 1-year overall survival in metastatic pancreatic cancer patients treated with nivolumab + chemotherapy (gem/nab-paclitaxel, PRINCE arm A1, n = 34 randomized, n = 25 with baseline CyTOF, n = 21 classifiable for 1-year OS plus 4 censored before day 365 retained in Cox models):

FAVORABLE DIRECTION (higher baseline frequency -> longer survival):
1. Tbet+ TCR-gamma-delta+ T cells (Tbet+ TCRgd+ T cells, % of TCRgd T cells; baseline median 0.79): strongest signal. Per-SD Cox HR 0.31 (95% CI 0.16-0.60, p = 0.0005; Holm-adjusted across 7 populations p = 0.0035). Kaplan-Meier median split: 1-year OS 0.89 (high) vs 0.42 (low), log-rank p = 0.0067. Also significant in a pooled 3-arm analysis with arm adjustment (HR 0.53, p = 0.006) and after Holm correction for the dichotomous endpoint (p = 0.024).
2. NKT cells (% of leukocytes; baseline median ~1.6e-2): per-SD odds ratio 5.56 for being alive at 1 year (logistic p = 0.025); per-SD Cox HR 0.48 (p = 0.008; Holm p = 0.050). Median split: 1-year OS 1.00 (high) vs 0.33 (low), log-rank p = 0.0017; 11 of 13 NKT-low patients died within 1 year.
3. Tbet+ T cells (% of CD3+ T cells; baseline median 0.18): per-SD Cox HR 0.54 (p = 0.033); median split 1-year OS 0.79 vs 0.50, log-rank p = 0.0075. Consistent but weaker in the pooled sensitivity analysis (HR 0.69, p = 0.042).

UNFAVORABLE DIRECTION (higher baseline frequency -> worse survival):
4. Ki-67+ cycling T cells (% of CD3+ T cells; baseline median 0.95, inverse marker): per-SD odds ratio 0.022 (logistic p = 0.050), per-SD Cox HR 2.28 (p = 0.044); median split 1-year OS 0.36 (high) vs 0.90 (low), log-rank p = 0.034. This signal was not reproduced in the pooled all-arms analysis (HR 1.27, p = 0.27) and is the least robust of the four.

NOT ASSOCIATED with 1-year OS in this cohort: HLA-DR+ non-naive (activated-memory) CD4 T cells, HLA-DR+ non-naive CD8 T cells, and total HLA-DR+ T cells (all Cox p >= 0.29; cross-validated AUCs 0.34-0.41). A prespecified multivariable model of the conventional activation axis (Tbet+ CD3+ plus HLA-DR+ CD4/CD8) was globally non-significant (LR p = 0.054, CV AUC 0.644).

KEY CONTEXT:
- The four signals form a single correlated immune axis (NKT vs Ki-67 Spearman rho = -0.91; NKT vs Tbet+ rho = 0.85), i.e., patients with a higher baseline innate-like, T-bet-expressing type-1 T cell compartment and a lower fraction of cycling peripheral T cells lived past 1 year on nivo/chemo. A post-hoc composite of NKT + Tbet+ gamma-delta + Ki-67 gave LR p = 0.002 with cross-validated out-of-fold AUC 0.779 (hypothesis-generating only, because the markers were selected on the same data).
- Associations are PROGNOSTIC, not proven predictive: no arm x marker interaction was detectable across the nivo/chemo, sotigalimab/chemo and triple-combination arms (all interaction p >= 0.088), so these populations likely track general host immune fitness in this chemo-immunotherapy setting.
- Limitations: single-arm focus within a small randomized phase-2 dataset (n = 21-25), 9/34 arm-A1 patients lacked baseline CyTOF and had shorter survival (median OS 303 vs 445 days, log-rank p = 0.12), 4 patients censored before day 365 were unclassifiable for the dichotomous endpoint, the deep T cell panel exists only at baseline (C1D1) so no kinetic biomarkers could be assessed, no external validation, and all inference is exploratory (Holm correction applied only within the prespecified 7-marker families). These markers require prospective validation before clinical use.
da-9-1.notes: Strong data loading, feature selection, biological interpretation, and sourcing, but cohort filtering used Arm instead of Actual Arm with a patient-count mismatch, survival methodology did not apply median-split log-rank to all features, and some p-values diverged from expected values.

da-9-7.answer:
No. At the on-treatment C2D1 timepoint of the PRINCE trial, circulating immune-cell frequencies (CyTOF) do not significantly correlate with serum protein levels (Olink NPX).

Evidence (patient-level Spearman correlations, paired by Deidentified.ID, BH-FDR across the 16 testable pairs):
- Only 4 CyTOF populations and 4 Olink proteins have C2D1 measurements: populations = Conventional DC (n=73), CCR7+ CD11b+ CD27- B cells, HLA-DR+ Non-Naive CD4 T Cells, HLA-DR+ Non-Naive CD8 T Cells (n=65 each); proteins = CXCL9, CXCL10, IFN-gamma, Soluble PD-1 (n=90 each). 73 patients have both modalities at C2D1.
- All 16 correlations are weak and non-significant: |rho| <= 0.233, minimum raw p = 0.0615, minimum FDR = 0.54. Strongest trends: B-cell frequency x CXCL9 (rho = -0.233, p = 0.062) and x CXCL10 (rho = -0.222, p = 0.076); HLA-DR+ non-naive CD4/CD8 T-cell frequency x soluble PD-1 (rho ~ +0.16, ns).
- The null is robust: unchanged using %leuk-denominator-only CyTOF samples (min FDR = 0.63), using Pearson on NPX, or stratifying by treatment arm (A1/B2/C2).
- The same pipeline at baseline (C1D1, 78 paired patients, 364 pairs) does find FDR-significant correlations (e.g., HLA-DR+ T cells x IL-8: rho = -0.43, FDR = 0.030), so the C2D1 null is not a pipeline artifact.
- Power: with n = 65-73, only moderate-or-stronger correlations (|rho| >= ~0.35) are detectable, so weak coupling cannot be excluded.

Conclusion: On-treatment at C2D1, the four measured circulating immune-cell frequencies carry no detectable, multiplicity-controlled association with CXCL9, CXCL10, IFN-gamma, or soluble PD-1 serum levels; they appear to be non-redundant, uncorrelated readouts at this timepoint. Any C2D1 correlation weaker than |rho| ~ 0.35 would be missed at this sample size, and conclusions are limited to the 16 feature pairs measurable at C2D1.
da-9-7.notes: The agent performed a careful pooled C2D1 correlation analysis with data validation and robustness checks, but the scope diverged from the expected 3x4 feature matrix and omitted full per-arm stratification, leading to the missed Arm C2 FDR-significant finding.

da-10-1.answer:
QUESTIONS
Using the provided self-assembling, partner-dependent, non-phase-separating protein sets (SaPS, PdPS, and NoPS) and the human proteome (hSaPS, hPdPS, hNoPS), compare amino-acid composition differences between PS-Self and PS-Part proteins, and evaluate the performance of four phase-separation predictors (PScore, PLAAC, catGRANULE, and FuzDrop) in distinguishing each PS type from non-PS proteins.

DATA
sequence_prediction_filtered.xlsx: 48,504 proteins x 23 columns (sequences, predictor scores, SaPS/hSaPS/PdPS/hPdPS/NoPS/hNoPS labels). Set sizes: SaPS 128, hSaPS 59, PdPS 214, hPdPS 96, NoPS 48,158, hNoPS 8,801; sets are disjoint. FuzDrop is NOT present in the file (verified by raw XML scan), so only PScore, PLAAC and catGRANULE could be evaluated; FuzDrop = unavailable.

1) AMINO-ACID COMPOSITION: PS-SELF (SaPS) VS PS-PART (PdPS)
Two-sided Mann-Whitney U per residue, Benjamini-Hochberg FDR; effect size as rank-biserial AUC (P(SaPS > PdPS)).

Benchmark sets (128 vs 214) — 13 of 20 residues differ at q < 0.05:
- HIGHER in SaPS (PS-Self): G +2.86 pp (mean 9.37% vs 6.52%; AUC 0.70, q = 5e-12), P +1.29 pp (7.38% vs 6.09%; AUC 0.60, q = 0.003), Q +0.79 pp (AUC 0.60, q = 0.005), S +0.96 pp (AUC 0.59, q = 0.008); Q+N combined AUC 0.60.
- LOWER in SaPS (i.e. higher in PdPS/PS-Part): L −1.62 pp (7.01% vs 8.63%; AUC 0.32, q = 2e-12), K −1.31 pp (5.48% vs 6.80%; AUC 0.36, q = 1e-4), E −1.13 pp (6.43% vs 7.56%; AUC 0.37, q = 1e-4), I −0.90 pp (AUC 0.35), D −0.72 pp (AUC 0.39), R −0.75 pp (AUC 0.43), V −0.46 pp (AUC 0.41), C −0.32 pp (AUC 0.39), H −0.33 pp (AUC 0.39).
- Net charge: FCR (D+E+K+R) is LOWER in SaPS, 22.2% vs 26.1% (AUC 0.33, q = 3e-6); NCPR does not differ significantly (AUC 0.54, q = 0.30) — SaPS proteins are less charged overall, not differently net-charged.
- Protein length does not differ (median 602 vs 565 aa, AUC 0.54, q = 0.25).
- Human subsets confirm the signature with smaller n (59 vs 96): G +2.55 pp (AUC 0.67, q = 0.005), E −1.37 pp (AUC 0.35, q = 0.009), K −1.42 pp (AUC 0.36, q = 0.013), L −1.62 pp (AUC 0.33, q = 0.005), FCR −4.2 pp (AUC 0.30, q = 4e-4); P and Q trend the same direction (AUC 0.59, q ≈ 0.18).

Interpretation: PS-Self proteins are enriched for the "low-complexity sticker-spacer" alphabet — glycine-rich, proline- and glutamine/asparagine-containing, with depleted hydrophobic/aliphatic bulk (L, I, V) and depleted charged residues (K, E, D, R) — consistent with self-association driven by multivalent weak interactions of prion-like/pliable low-complexity domains (e.g. FUS, hnRNPA1, TAF15). PS-Part (PdPS) proteins keep more conventional folded-domain chemistry (higher L/I/V hydrophobicity and higher K/E/D charge), consistent with phase separation that requires partners (RNA, SH3/PRM-type modules) rather than intrinsic self-adhesion of an IDR.

2) PREDICTOR PERFORMANCE, PS TYPE VS NON-PS (ROC-AUC; higher score = more PS-like)
                         SaPS vs NoPS   PdPS vs NoPS   hSaPS vs hNoPS   hPdPS vs hNoPS   SaPS vs PdPS
PScore                       0.831          0.662           0.813            0.689            0.702
PLAAC                        0.834          0.644           0.831            0.640            0.719
catGRANULE                   0.817          0.706           0.813            0.726            0.665
FuzDrop                 unavailable    unavailable     unavailable      unavailable      unavailable
Reference mechanism-specific classifiers (provided in the file):
SaPS-8fea / SaPS-10fea       0.982 / 0.990  0.754 / 0.784   0.987 / 0.990    0.783 / 0.788    0.905 / 0.895 (positive class SaPS)
PdPS-8fea / PdPS-10fea       0.841 / 0.913  0.973 / 0.990   0.850 / 0.915    0.984 / 0.990    0.137–0.205 (AUC for SaPS; i.e. ~0.79–0.87 reversed for PdPS)

All three p-values for "score higher in PS class than NoPS" are < 1e-10 (one-sided Mann-Whitney). PR metrics are heavily class-imbalanced (NoPS base rates 0.3–1.1%): PR-AUC fold-over-random for SaPS tasks is 8–18x (e.g. PScore hSaPS PR-AUC 0.131 vs base 0.0073, 17.8x) but only ~2.5x for PdPS tasks; precision in the top 1% of the ranking reaches 5.1–22.7% for SaPS vs 1.9–8.8% for PdPS.

Per-organism: SaPS discrimination is consistently strong (AUC 0.70–0.98 across 10 organisms; e.g. Arabidopsis PScore 0.983, rat catGRANULE 0.960) while PdPS discrimination is weak and inconsistent (AUC 0.38–0.97, median ~0.66; catGRANULE 0.384 in Xenopus, PLAAC 0.443 in Arabidopsis).

3) KEY CONCLUSIONS
(a) Composition separates the two PS mechanisms: SaPS = G/S/P/Q-rich, L/I/V- and charge-depleted ("sticker-spacer" low-complexity chemistry); PdPS = higher L/I/V and K/E/D, i.e. more globular, charged and hydrophobic.
(b) All three evaluated general PS predictors (PScore, PLAAC, catGRANULE) discriminate SELF-assembling PS proteins well (AUC ≈ 0.81–0.83 human, up to 0.98 in some organisms) but partner-dependent PS proteins poorly (AUC ≈ 0.64–0.73 human). catGRANULE is the single best of the three on PdPS (0.706 all-organisms / 0.726 human); PLAAC and PScore are marginally best on SaPS (0.834 / 0.831 all-organisms). FuzDrop was not in the provided data and could not be scored.
(c) Consequently the three general predictors also partially separate SaPS from PdPS (AUC 0.67–0.73), because they inherit the composition bias of self-assembling IDRs.
(d) The provided mechanism-aware 8/10-feature classifiers reach AUC 0.97–0.99 for their own mechanism vs NoPS and AUC ≈ 0.90–0.92 for SaPS vs PdPS, showing that composition-derived features carry the mechanistic signal; general PS predictors capture only the SaPS half of it.
(e) Practical implication for MLO-participant screening: high PScore/PLAAC/catGRANULE scores flag candidates for SELF-assembling condensate proteins, but a low score does NOT exclude partner-dependent participation (e.g. PdPS scaffold proteins that enter condensates via RNA or modular interactions); screening pipelines should pair predictor scores with partner-interaction evidence.

CAVEATS
FuzDrop unavailable in the provided files; PScore missing for 4,653/48,504 rows (short-protein bias, 0 missing among SaPS); the 10-feature scores exist only for the 8,954 human rows; NoPS/hNoPS are heterogeneous "rest-of-proteome" negatives, so metrics measure discrimination from the generic proteome rather than from verified non-PS controls; the 8/10-feature classifiers were trained on these protein families, so their near-perfect AUCs are optimistic (in-family) estimates; MLO/BioID localization labels referenced in the task preamble are not present in the provided workbooks.
da-10-1.notes: The agent performed a thorough end-to-end analysis with strong data verification, dataset construction, predictor AUC evaluation, and interpretation. Main gaps are the lack of global amino-acid frequency pooling, absence of fold-change computation, and non-use of IDR data despite availability, leading to B/C on some composition-related criteria.

da-10-3.answer:
ANSWER: Yes — but with two qualifications (strength depends on the predictor family, and part of the apparent gap in the raw benchmark is training-set circularity).

Evidence (negatives = fixed hNoPS-test background, n = 8,172 hNoPS proteins absent from the MLO list; positives = members of each dataset):

1) Per-dataset screening performance (within the 8,956-protein master table) is consistently higher for the four MLO participant sets than for the membrane-bound control (human mitochondrial proteome) for every predictor. All 8 predictors x 4 MLO sets x mito control = 32/32 paired comparisons have dAUROC = AUROC(MLO) - AUROC(mito) > 0; 27/32 significant at one-sided permutation p < 0.05 (paired bootstrap CIs exclude 0 in the same 27); predictor-level sign test p = 0.0039. Mean dAUROC over the 4 MLO sets: PScore +0.188, PLAAC +0.200, catGRANULE +0.201, DeepPhase +0.080, SaPS-8fea +0.271, PdPS-8fea +0.305, SaPS-10fea +0.330, PdPS-10fea +0.296.

2) Representative AUROC values (vs hNoPS-test): PdPS-10fea reaches 0.703 (OpenCell punctae), 0.782 (DACT1 particulate), 0.845 (G3BP1 proximity), 0.982 (PhaSepDB) versus 0.532 on the mitochondrial control; SaPS-10fea 0.613-0.942 vs 0.454. The mito control is actually anti-correlated with PS-like composition (PLAAC 0.416, PScore 0.410, top-1% enrichment log2 -2.4): mitochondrial proteins are depleted of IDR/low-complexity, condensate-forming features, which is exactly what makes it a specificity control.

3) Ranking across MLO sets is stable: ML classifiers (SaPS/PdPS) > catGRANULE > PLAAC ~= PScore > DeepPhase; 10-feature versions beat 8-feature versions on every dataset; PdPS >= SaPS on nearly all sets. Dataset difficulty within the MLO family: PhaSepDB high-throughput (0.75-0.98) > G3BP1 proximity (0.49-0.85) > OpenCell punctae (0.56-0.70) > DACT1 particulate (0.45-0.78).

4) Qualification 1 — circularity: the within-master PhaSepDB positives are 24 SaPS + 41 PdPS + 0 NoPS, i.e. mostly training members of the ML classifiers, which inflates ML scores on that set. Re-running the benchmark on the full "Training proteins removed" positives (OpenCell 115, DACT1 219, G3BP1 234, PhaSepDB 1,597, mito 1,120, amyloid 45) scored in the cross-species prediction table leaves the conclusion intact but shrinks it: ML classifiers keep AUROC 0.63-0.84 on MLO sets vs 0.47-0.56 on the mito control (mean over 4 MLO sets: SaPS-8fea 0.641, PdPS-8fea 0.668, SaPS-10fea 0.738, PdPS-10fea 0.801), while PScore/PLAAC drop to ~chance (0.33-0.52), showing their raw apparent advantage was largely carried by SaPS/PdPS members inside the MLO sets.

5) Qualification 2 — the amyloid fiber-forming set (aggregation control, not membrane-bound) separates the predictor families: vs amyloid the MLO advantage is 28/32 positive (sign test p = 0.035) but significant in only 16/32, and PScore (and occasionally PLAAC/DeepPhase) is NOT better on MLO sets than on amyloid (e.g. PScore/DACT1 dAUROC = -0.163). Only the ML classifiers beat the amyloid control consistently (4/4 sets for all four SaPS/PdPS scores).

Conclusion: Screening performance is consistently (32/32 comparisons, p = 0.0039) better on MLO participant datasets than on the membrane-bound organelle control, for all eight predictors, and this holds after removing training proteins for the ML scores (0.63-0.84 vs 0.47-0.56 AUROC). The margin is largest for the supervised SaPS/PdPS classifiers (especially the 10-feature versions, PdPS-10fea best) and modest for legacy scores on the hardest sets. AUPRC at 0.5% prevalence stays low in absolute terms (0.03-0.40 for ML scores), so the scores enrich MLO participants reliably relative to membrane-bound organelle proteins but are not stand-alone classifiers. Caveats: positives are membership labels from ensemble/proteomic studies (including indirect binders), the negative set is operational (hNoPS by the same classification scheme), and the PhaSepDB column remains mildly homology-contaminated even after training-protein removal.
da-10-3.notes: The agent's work meets the highest level for all criteria: correct identification of inputs, label construction, missing data handling, AUC computation, quantitative comparison with clear conclusion, and reliable sourcing.

da-11-1.answer:
FINAL ANSWER — Top signaling pathways predicted to mediate KIR+CD8+ T-cell suppression and cytotoxic targeting of CD4+ T cells in active celiac mucosa (beyond the MHC-I → CD3/CD8 baseline)

Cohort analyzed from the provided raw data: 10 mucosal biopsies (6 active CeD, 4 HC, GSE193442), 72,177 cells loaded; 56,586 cells x 15,835 genes after QC; Leiden clustering into 21 states. The KIR+ cytotoxic compartment was defined as cells with >=1 UMI across KIR2DL1/KIR2DL2DL3/KIR2DL4/KIR3DL1/KIR3DL2 within the 10 cytotoxic/gamma-delta clusters: 2,119 cells in CeD vs 585 in HC (3.6x expansion), strongly armed (GZMB 91%, PRF1 95%, GNLY 85%, FCGR3A +2.31 logFC vs KIR- cells, NKG2A/KLRC1 +2.41), with a CD8alpha-alpha / gamma-delta-IEL-like character (TRDC+ 38%, TRDV2+ 70%, CD8A+ 34%). CD4+ targets: 21,054 CeD vs 10,184 HC cells (2.1x expansion), activated (HLA-C +0.84, CD48, CXCR4, CCR7 up). Ligand-receptor inference used liana rank_aggregate (consensus of CellPhoneDB/NATMI/Connectome/SingleCellSignalR/logFC/geometric-mean; expr_prop 0.05, 1,000 permutations, seed 0), run separately per condition, direction KIR+CD8 -> CD4, with KIR- cytotoxic cells and the HC condition as controls, followed by a per-sample pseudobulk validation (n=6 CeD vs n=4 HC).

MHC-I (HLA-A/B/C -> CD3D/CD8A/CD8B) was recovered as the strongest baseline interaction (lr_means 0.81-0.86), as expected. The top pathways BEYOND MHC-I, ranked by combining significance in KIR+CD8-CeD -> CD4-CeD (56 of 89 pairs significant at permutation p <= 0.05), CeD specificity (46/56 pairs stronger in CeD), KIR+ specificity (49/56 pairs stronger from KIR+ than KIR- sources), and pseudobulk validation:

1. FASLG -> FAS / TNFRSF1A (death-receptor apoptosis) — the leading suppressive/cytotoxic candidate. FASLG in 10.0% of KIR+CD8-CeD vs 4.1% of KIR-CD8-CeD and 2.2% of KIR+CD8-HC; both FAS and TNFRSF1A pairs significant in CeD (permutation p = 0.0); per-donor ligand x receptor product is 6.9-fold higher in CeD than HC (0.0030 vs 0.0004; Welch p = 0.053, Mann-Whitney p = 0.067 at n=6 vs 4; every CeD-vs-HC comparison directional). Predicts Fas-mediated apoptosis of Fas+ CD4 targets as the main in-vitro killing route besides perforin/granzyme.

2. CCL5/CCL4 -> CXCR3 / CCR5 / DPP4 (effector chemokine axis) — strongest non-MHC-I magnitude among significant pairs (CCL5->DPP4 rank 0.364, CCL5->CXCR3 0.369, both p = 0.0) and the most KIR+-specific signals in the network (KIR+ specificity delta +0.080 and +0.081). CCL4 in 89% and CCL5 in 99% of KIR+CD8-CeD. Function: recruitment of chemokine-receptor+ CD4 cells into the effector-target contact zone rather than direct killing.

3. LGALS1 (galectin-1) -> CD45/PTPRC, CD69, ITGB1 (immunoregulatory lectin) — significant in CeD (p = 0.0), high in BOTH specificity contrasts (delta_CeD +0.028..+0.039; delta_KIR+ +0.048..+0.077), pseudobulk 2.0x in CeD (p = 0.059). The strongest candidate for active suppression of CD4 responses beyond cytotoxicity (galectin-1 induces T-cell apoptosis/tolerance).

4. MHC-II (HLA-DPB1/DQA1/DRB1/DQB1) -> CD4 — "MHC beyond MHC-I". KIR+ cells transcribe HLA-DPB1 (61%), HLA-DQA1 (49%), HLA-DRB1 (26%); HLA-DRB1->CD4 is the #2 CeD-specific pair overall (delta_CeD +0.043, delta_KIR+ +0.041; pseudobulk 2.15x). Direct killer-to-target contact; the proposed inhibitory MHC-II -> LAG3 route is only partially supported (LAG3 on 20% of KIR+ cells but receiver-side pairs not significant).

Tier 2: TGFB1 -> CXCR4/CD44 (TGFB1 in 50% of KIR+CD8-CeD; the only axis with pseudobulk p < 0.05, 1.39x, p = 0.046 — but weakest source attribution since Tregs also produce it); HMGB1 -> CXCR4 (delta_CeD +0.033, pseudobulk 1.34x, p = 0.062, alarmin-guided recruitment); TIMP1 -> CD63 (#1 CeD-specific pair, delta +0.055); FAM3C -> CLEC2D (LLT1) (novel inferred trans-inhibitory contact, delta +0.030).

Tier 3 (contact/co-stimulation): ITGB2 (LFA-1) -> CD226 (DNAM-1) (+0.041 KIR+-specific), SELPLG -> SELL/ITGB2, ADA/PAM -> DPP4. Explicit negatives: MIF -> CD44/CD74 and VIM -> CD44 are NOT KIR+- or CeD-specific (negative deltas) despite high magnitude; CD48 -> CD2 is generic T-T contact; HLA-E -> NKG2A-type autocrine circuitry not recoverable in target direction (permutation p = 1.0).

Overall interpretation: in active CeD the expanded KIR+ cytotoxic pool is wired for (i) contact-dependent killing of CD4 targets chiefly through FASLG-FAS (plus its granzyme/perforin program, expression-only evidence), (ii) chemokine-driven engagement of CXCR3/CCR5/DPP4+ CD4 cells, and (iii) suppression beyond killing through galectin-1, TGF-beta1, MHC-II-mediated contact and an LLT1/CLEC2D-type inhibitory axis.

Caveats: gliadin-specific CD4 cells cannot be identified from scRNA alone (targets = disease-enriched CD4 compartment); L-R inference is correlational and permutation treats cells as exchangeable (pseudobulk with n=6 vs 4 is conservative; FASLG axis p = 0.053); one CeD donor contributes 1,539/2,119 KIR+ cells; the KIR+ pool is CD8alpha-alpha/gamma-delta-like rather than pure alpha-beta CD8; myeloid/epithelial/stromal sources are absent (purified lymphocyte fraction), limiting cytokine axes (e.g., IFNG -> IFNGR: IFNG only 3% of KIR+ cells); KIR/HLA genotypes unavailable.

Evidence: all numbers from this run's outputs (trace.md section 4; tables under ccc-kir-cd8/output/tables/ including liana_focus_CeD.csv, pairwise_comparison_KIRplus.csv, axis_summary.csv, pseudobulk_group_stats.csv; methods in ccc-kir-cd8/README.md). Key external mechanisms: Strasser et al., Immunity 2009 (FAS); Rabinovich & Toscano, Nat Rev Immunol 2009 and Perillo et al., Nature 1995 (galectin-1); Li & Flavell, Cell 2008 (TGF-beta); Groom & Luster, Exp Cell Res 2011 (CXCR3); Meresse et al., Immunity 2004 / J Exp Med 2006 and Jabri & Sollid, Nat Rev Immunol 2009 (cytotoxic IEL biology in CeD); Efremova et al., NAR 2020 and Dimitrov et al., Nat Commun 2022 (inference methods).
da-11-1.notes: The analysis is largely rigorous with careful QC, clustering, LR inference, and pathway ranking. However, omitted activated CD4 marker scoring, used a fixed rather than data-driven KIR threshold, did not identify gliadin-specific CD4 cells, and did not compute the reverse communication direction, preventing top marks in those criteria.

da-12-2.answer:
Answer: YES — marginally. The G2M checkpoint is enriched among the 1,543 DEGs shared between the overexpression and knockdown experiments at the raw p < 0.05 level, but the signal is modest and does not survive multiple-testing correction.

Evidence:
- Shared DEGs (marked "v" in both overlap-flag columns of TS7.xlsx): 1,543 genes.
- Background universe: union of both DEG lists = 7,005 unique genes (3,260 OE + 5,290 KD).
- HALLMARK_G2M_CHECKPOINT: 200 genes, 121 present in the background.
- Observed G2M members among shared DEGs: 37 (e.g. PTTG3P, SMC4, NOTCH2, SMC1A, ATRX, TOP2A, INCENP, BRCA2, LMNB1, ESPL1) vs 26.7 expected by chance = 1.39-fold enrichment.
- One-sided hypergeometric p = 0.0171 (< 0.05); Fisher exact OR = 1.57, p = 0.0266; permutation p = 0.031 (10,000 label shuffles).
- The p < 0.05 call is robust to the background-universe choice (p = 0.017 union DEGs; 0.041 coding-like genes only; 5.3e-07 illustrative whole-genome background) and to including 2 extra unflagged cross-list overlap genes (p = 0.0175). It fails only for the most restrictive background (GMT-covered genes only, p > 0.999).
- Caveat: across all 50 supplied Hallmark sets, only 2 survive BH-FDR < 0.05 (HALLMARK_MITOTIC_SPINDLE, FDR = 1.2e-06; HALLMARK_UV_RESPONSE_DN, FDR = 0.0047); G2M ranks 3rd of 50 with FDR = 0.286, i.e. not significant after multiple-testing correction.
- Note: all 1,543 shared DEGs are anti-correlated between the two experiments (100% up in overexpression / down in knockdown), consistent with a dose-dependent ncRNA-responsive program of which G2M cell-cycle genes are one modest component.

Conclusion: under the question's stated criterion (p < 0.05), yes, the G2M checkpoint is enriched among the shared DEGs (fold 1.39, hypergeometric p = 0.017); however, this is nominal significance only — after Benjamini-Hochberg correction over the 50 tested Hallmark pathways the enrichment is not significant (FDR = 0.286), so G2M is a weak, secondary signal (the dominant shared signal is mitotic spindle assembly).
da-12-2.notes: The agent performed a thorough, source-grounded ORA with correct gene extraction and methodology, though its quantitative G2M results deviate from expected values and its top-pathway reporting is incomplete.

da-12-4.answer:
No — not robustly. In the task-mandated univariate Cox PH screen of all tumor-microbiome taxa in the matched TCGA-LUAD cohort (457 samples with microbiome + survival data, 173 deaths), Kocuria nominally meets the poor-prognosis definition (HR > 1 and p < 0.05): z-scored counts give HR = 1.124 per SD (95% CI 1.013–1.247), p = 0.0274, making it one of 12 of 226 testable taxa flagged as poor-prognosis (alongside Finegoldia, Peptoniphilus, Bilophila, Gardnerella, Anaerococcus, Sutterella, etc.). However, the association does not hold up under scrutiny:

1. Multiple testing: Benjamini-Hochberg FDR across the 226 taxa gives q = 0.70 for Kocuria — not significant. ~11 false positives are expected among 226 tests at alpha = 0.05.
2. Single-sample artifact: the nominal signal is driven by one extreme sample (TCGA-05-4402-01A, 99.5 collapsed Kocuria reads, death at 244 days). Removing it yields HR = 0.988 (95% CI 0.899–1.085), p = 0.799.
3. Normalization sensitivity: log1p-transformed counts give HR = 1.108 (0.813–1.510), p = 0.517.
4. Biologically meaningful contrast: presence/absence Cox model (51 Kocuria-positive vs 406 Kocuria-negative tumors) gives HR = 1.126 (0.730–1.736), p = 0.592; median-split Kaplan-Meier curves are barely separated (median OS 1073 vs 1265 days), log-rank p = 0.593.

Biological context: Kocuria is a skin/mucosal commensal and occasional opportunistic pathogen; its sparse detection in low-biomass tumor data (90% of samples negative) fits a contamination/reagent-DNA pattern reported for TCGA-derived microbiome tables rather than a true intratumoral colonizer.

Conclusion: By the literal screening criterion (HR > 1, p < 0.05), Kocuria is nominally flagged, but the association is not statistically robust (fails FDR, driven by a single sample, vanishes under log transform and presence/absence coding). The data do not support Kocuria as a significantly poor-prognosis-associated microbe in this cohort; the only taxa whose nominal signal survives BH-FDR are the correlated skin-flora anaerobes Finegoldia and Peptoniphilus (both q = 0.007), and even these rest on unadjusted univariate models with no clinical covariates available.
da-12-4.notes: The analysis pipeline is sound and complete, but the final Kocuria conclusion diverges from the task's explicit HR>1 and p<0.05 significance definition, which prevents full credit on criterion 4.

da-13-1.answer:
Answer: Yes — 6 months of feminizing GAHT significantly remodels the plasma proteome (dominated by broad decreases), and the changes differ between the CPA and SPIRO antiandrogen regimens in both magnitude of shared effects and in arm-specific proteins.

Analysis summary (paired design, 40 subjects x baseline/6 months; 20 per arm; 4,897 detectable Olink Explore HT assays out of 5,420; BH FDR):

1) Proteins significantly altered after 6 months (within-regimen paired t-tests on DeltaNPX):
- CPA arm: 268/4,897 assays at BH q<0.05 — 256 decreased, 12 increased.
  Largest decreases: SPINT3 -7.91 NPX, INSL3 -5.34, EDDM3B -2.67, TEX101 -2.08, RBP1 -2.04, ACRV1 -1.37.
  Increases: CXCL13 +1.84 (q=1e-4), LEP +1.50 (q=1e-4), PRL +1.38 (q~1e-5).
- SPIRO arm: 129/4,897 at BH q<0.05 — 126 decreased, 3 increased.
  Largest decreases: SPINT3 -3.52 (q=0.006), ATP5F1D -2.86 (q=0.043), INSL3 -1.75 (q=0.016), EDDM3B -1.32 (q=0.006), TEX101 -0.91 (q=0.034).
  Significant increase: LEP +1.04 (q=0.028).
- Both arms shift globally downward (70.8% / 77.8% of assays negative; Wilcoxon signed-rank p~1e-221 and <1e-300).

2) Regimen x time interaction (does the change differ between CPA and SPIRO?):
Two-stage Welch contrast (delta_SPIRO - delta_CPA, BH-corrected) finds 10 proteins at q<0.05; a full per-assay mixed model NPX ~ time*regimen + (1|subject) confirms them and adds 17 more at q<0.05 (the two interaction p-value vectors agree at Spearman rho = 0.9999). Headline interaction hits (Delta CPA vs Delta SPIRO; positive delta_diff = CPA falls more):
- INSL3: -5.34 vs -1.75 (diff +3.60, q=2e-5) — Leydig-cell hormone under LH control; CPA suppresses the HPG axis far more strongly.
- SPINT3: -7.91 vs -3.52 (diff +4.39, q=0.004).
- PRL: +1.38 vs +0.19 (diff -1.19, q=4e-5) — prolactin rises only under CPA, consistent with its dopamine-D2 antagonism.
- CXCL13: +1.84 vs +0.21 (diff -1.63, q=0.004) — CPA-specific B-cell chemokine signal.
- NELL1, CFC1, SPOCK1, EDDM3B, RTBDN, REN complete the q<0.05 set; REN falls under CPA (-0.56) but rises under SPIRO (+0.19), matching spironolactone's known hyperreninemic mineralocorticoid-receptor blockade.
Overlap between arms: 52 proteins significant in both arms at q<0.05, 52/52 in the same direction (51 down), a ~10-fold enrichment over chance (5.4 expected), but the global per-protein response vectors correlate at only Spearman rho = 0.044 — a shared androgen-dependent core (INSL3, SPINT3, TEX101, EDDM3B, ACRV1, MSMB, PROK1, MUC1, CA6 all down in both; LEP up in both) plus large regimen-specific components.

Biological interpretation: CPA suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, collapsing LH-dependent secretion (INSL3 3x lower than SPIRO, deeper falls in epididymal/seminal proteins) and, uniquely, increases prolactin; spironolactone's peripheral androgen-receptor blockade produces qualitatively similar but milder shared changes plus a distinct renin response. Concordant rises in leptin and SHBG-like liver markers reflect estrogen-driven adiposity and hepatic effects common to both regimens.

Key limitations: 20 pairs per arm (interaction tests modestly powered); no covariate data (age, BMI, estrogen dose, gonadotropins); single plate (no batch adjustment possible); LOD reconstructed from negative-control wells because the LOD column is empty in the export (results robust across detection-filter choices); 4 SDRF timepoint labels contradicted sample-ID suffixes and were adjudicated by suffix (PCA-supported, 40/40 pairing restored); observational design — no randomization between antiandrogens.
da-13-1.notes: The agent delivered a methodologically rigorous, well-documented differential expression analysis that correctly handles paired design, multiple testing, regimen comparison, biological interpretation, and source reliability, with only minor potential omissions such as not explicitly stating CPA-unique and SPIRO-unique counts.

da-13-3.answer:
Question: Which proteins correlate with changes in body composition (fat percentage and breast volume) following feminizing GAHT?

Data: 5,278 plasma proteins (Olink Explore-HT) tested for mixed-linear-model association (random intercept per participant; adjusted for age and baseline BMI) with percent body fat and with breast volume. Significance threshold: Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p < 0.05.

HEADLINE NUMBERS
- Percent body fat: 38 significant proteins (2 positive, 36 negative); 11 at adj p < 0.01.
- Breast volume: 249 significant proteins (12 positive, 237 negative); 78 at adj p < 0.01.
- Overlap between traits: 28 proteins significant for both (Fisher exact OR = 63.6, p = 5.1e-30); effect directions are concordant in 28/28. Genome-wide Spearman correlation of the two association profiles: rho = +0.28 (p = 1.8e-93).
- Total distinct proteins significantly associated with at least one trait: 259 of 5,278 (4.9%).

PERCENT BODY FAT — PROTEINS AND ASSOCIATIONS
Positive (higher protein with higher fat %):
- LEP (leptin): beta = +0.196, adj p = 5.5e-4 — the single strongest fat hit; canonical adipocyte-derived adiposity marker.
- CFC1: beta = +0.071, adj p = 0.025 — EGF-CFC developmental signaling co-receptor.
Negative (higher protein with lower fat %; strongest 15 by effect size):
- MAPK4: -0.217 (adj p 0.047)
- DEFB4A (beta-defensin 4A): -0.209 (0.014)
- MUC1 (epithelial mucin): -0.167 (0.015)
- CA6 (carbonic anhydrase VI, glandular secretion): -0.139 (5.5e-4; tied smallest p with LEP and PLB1)
- MMP3 (matrix metalloproteinase-3): -0.112 (0.015)
- CCL24 (eotaxin-2): -0.102 (0.0018)
- PSG1 (pregnancy-specific beta-1-glycoprotein): -0.098 (0.0029)
- PI3 / elafin (epithelial antiprotease): -0.096 (0.013)
- PPY (pancreatic polypeptide, satiety hormone): -0.094 (0.031)
- PGLYRP3 (peptidoglycan recognition protein 3): -0.085 (0.0029)
- PLB1 (phospholipase B1): -0.084 (5.5e-4)
- CYTL1: -0.076 (0.0029)
- IVL (involucrin): -0.074 (0.010)
- CST6 (cystatin E/M): -0.070 (0.0049)
- CLSTN2: -0.064 (0.021)
Further significant negatives: VIT, FGFBP2, ENDOU, SPINK5, CBLIF, SOST (sclerostin, Wnt antagonist), ENPP5, LY75, KLK13, IGSF21, DSG3, WIF1 (Wnt-inhibitory factor 1), ART3, RELT, XPNPEP2, DPEP1, KLK6, CEACAM19, ITGAV, COL15A1, CRTAC1.
Interpretation: the fat signature is dominated by inverse correlations with innate-immunity/granulocyte proteins (CCL24, PGLYRP3, DEFB4A, PI3, FGFBP2, CA6, KLK6), epithelial/glandular-secretory proteins (MUC1, IVL, DSG3, SPINK5, CST6) and ECM-remodeling/Wnt-antagonist proteins (MMP3, COL15A1, ITGAV, WIF1, SOST). LEP is the expected positive adiposity marker; the Wnt-antagonist decreases (WIF1, SOST) are permissive for adipogenesis in the Wnt-adipogenesis literature.

BREAST VOLUME — PROTEINS AND ASSOCIATIONS
Positive (higher protein with larger breast volume) — a coherent mammary-gland-activation signature:
- CXCL13: +0.00592, adj p 6.7e-4 — largest positive effect of all 249 hits.
- LEP (leptin): +0.00527, adj p 3.1e-3 — the only protein positively associated with BOTH traits.
- PRL (prolactin): +0.00435, adj p 2.8e-4 — master mammogenic hormone.
- PAEP (milk protein beta-lactoglobulin / glycodelin): +0.00249, adj p 0.030 — direct secretory-epithelium readout.
- CCL28 (+0.00215, 0.033), TNFAIP6 (+0.00160, 0.027), VEGFD (lymphangiogenic; +0.00107, 0.038), CD70 (+0.00107, 0.046), MZB1 (+0.00101, 0.045), EDA2R (+0.00088, 0.044), GAPDH (+0.00080, 0.0077), RAB27B (secretory GTPase; +0.00066, 0.049).
Negative (higher protein with smaller breast volume; strongest by effect size / significance):
- INSL3 (insulin-like 3, Leydig-cell androgen-responsive hormone): -0.01515, adj p = 3.3e-5 — the single most significant association in the entire table; direct endocrine readout of androgen/testicular suppression on GAHT.
- SPINT3: -0.02035, adj p 3.1e-4 (largest magnitude).
- Also: EDDM3B (epididymal protease inhibitor; -0.0069, 5.9e-4), TEX101 (testis-expressed; -0.0045, 0.025), DEFB4A (-0.0058), MUC1 (-0.0053), PROK1 (-0.0043), PM20D1 (-0.0043), MMP3 (-0.0035), CCK (-0.0036), NPY (-0.0039), TOP1, CUL7, MME, PTPRH, and ~220 more.
Interpretation: positive hits (PRL, PAEP, CXCL13, CCL28, MZB1, RAB27B, TNFAIP6, VEGFD) mark growing ductal-lobular tissue with secretory/lactational differentiation and accompanying mucosal lymphoid and lymphatic expansion. The dominant negative hits are male-reproductive-axis proteins (INSL3, TEX101, EDDM3B, SPINT3) collapsing under antiandrogen + estrogen therapy, plus broad ECM/metabolic declines.

PROTEINS SIGNIFICANT FOR BOTH TRAITS (28, all concordant in sign; 27 negative, LEP positive)
LEP (+/+), and concordant-negative: KLK6, CEACAM19, DPEP1, XPNPEP2, IGSF21, LY75, ENPP5, SOST, CBLIF, SPINK5, ENDOU, FGFBP2, VIT, CLSTN2, CST6, IVL, CYTL1, PLB1, PGLYRP3, PPY, PI3, PSG1, CCL24, MMP3, CA6, MUC1, DEFB4A.
LEP is the standout shared marker: secreted in proportion to fat mass and a known permissive factor in mammary ductal outgrowth, hence positively linked to both fat accretion and breast enlargement.

BIOLOGICAL SUMMARY
Feminizing GAHT body-composition change is accompanied by: (1) a leptin-scale increase tracking adipose accretion (LEP is the top and only strong positive fat hit); (2) emergence of a mammary secretory/glandular proteomic signature specific to breast volume (PRL, PAEP, CXCL13, CCL28, RAB27B, TNFAIP6, VEGFD); (3) suppression of androgen/testicular-axis proteins (INSL3 — most significant hit in the table — TEX101, EDDM3B, SPINT3); and (4) a broadly inverse systemic inflammatory/granulocyte and epithelial-secretory profile shared by both traits (CCL24, PGLYRP3, DEFB4A, PI3, MMP3, MUC1, CA6, CST6, CYTL1, PSG1...).

LIMITATIONS
- Correlational cross-sectional-style mixed-model coefficients (random intercept per participant, adjusted only for age and baseline BMI); no causal or temporal direction can be inferred from these numbers alone.
- Only adjusted p-values are provided (no raw p-values, confidence intervals, sample sizes, or per-arm CPA-vs-SPIRO coefficients); the authors' FDR cannot be recomputed or stratified.
- Breast-volume units are not stated in the file; effect magnitudes are not comparable across the two traits (only signs and within-trait ranks).
- At FDR 0.05 across 5,278 tests, roughly 2 of the 38 fat hits and 12 of the 249 breast-volume hits are expected false positives; hits near adj p ~ 0.05 should be treated cautiously, whereas LEP, INSL3, PRL, CXCL13, PAEP, CA6, CCL24, PGLYRP3 (adj p <= 1e-3) are individually robust.

Key references: Considine et al. 1996 (NEJM 334:292; PMID 8532024; leptin-fat proportionality); Ben-Jonathan et al. 2008 (Endocr Rev 29:1; PMID 18048726; prolactin mammogenic role); Hennighausen & Robinson 2005 (Nat Rev Mol Cell Biol 6:715; PMID 16136448; mammary gland networks); Ivell & Anand-Ivell 2018 (Hum Reprod Update 24:537; PMID 29246935; INSL3 as Leydig-cell androgen-responsive marker); Ross et al. 2000 (Science 289:950; PMID 10976015; Wnt suppression of adipogenesis); Benjamini & Hochberg 1995 (J R Stat Soc B 57:289; FDR methodology); UniProt (uniprot.org; protein function annotations).
da-13-3.notes: The agent's analysis is thorough, accurate, and well-documented, meeting all rubric criteria at the highest level.

da-13-5.notes: The agent performed careful data loading and biological interpretation but deviated from the required top-100 sex-associated protein analysis by using a threshold-based sex-associated set, which invalidated the expected overlap and enrichment results even though directional analysis was methodologically sound.

da-13-6.answer:
No. GAHT-induced protein changes are NOT consistent with those observed during menopause — they are predominantly ANTI-concordant with menopause and, instead, concordant with the protein signature of menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) and of higher endogenous estradiol. In other words, 6 months of feminizing GAHT shifts the plasma proteome in a premenopausal, estrogen-replete direction.

Evidence (Olink Explore-HT, 2,791 proteins shared between Supplementary Tables 1 and 7; GAHT set = 258 proteins with adjusted p<0.05 in the CPA and/or SPIRO arm; 225 down / 33 up):

1) Versus menopause (<57): anti-concordant.
- Only 38/258 (14.7%) of GAHT-changed proteins move in the same direction as the menopause association (two-sided exact binomial p = 2.5e-32 vs 50% expected).
- Mean menopause coefficient within the GAHT set is +0.0700 (one-sample Wilcoxon p = 3.0e-25): proteins that menopause RAISES are proteins GAHT LOWERS.
- 86.0% (222/258) of the GAHT set is significantly menopause-associated (enrichment vs 5% background, p = 3.2e-246), and among proteins significant in both analyses, 89.4% (160/179, CPA arm) and 83.6% (61/73, SPIRO arm) show OPPOSITE signs.
- Full-proteome Spearman rho(GAHT z-score, menopause estimate) = -0.186 (2,000-permutation p = 5.0e-4).
- Direction split: the anti-menopausal signal is driven by the 225 GAHT-down proteins, which are elevated in the menopause comparison (+0.0791, p = 3.6e-25).

2) Versus MHT: concordant.
- Sign concordance 72.1% (186/258) with MHT<57 (binomial p = 8.4e-13) and 80.2% (207/258) with MHT>=57 (p = 1.8e-23).
- 54.7% (141/258) and 45.3% (117/258) of the GAHT set is MHT-significant — a ~9.2-9.5-fold enrichment over the 5% background (p <= 7.0e-111).
- Among proteins significant in both GAHT (per arm) and MHT, 77-95% share the same sign (e.g., 84/109 CPA-MHT<57; 41/43 SPIRO-MHT>=57; Fisher p <= 9.1e-7). Full-proteome rho with MHT>=57 = +0.111 (perm p = 5.0e-4).

3) Versus endogenous estradiol in women (ln-E2): concordant — the strongest positive full-proteome correlation measured (Spearman rho = +0.169, perm p = 5.0e-4; 72.1% sign concordance in the GAHT set, p = 8.4e-13).

4) Versus testosterone: anti-concordant as mechanistically expected for an antiandrogen+estradiol regimen (sign concordance 31.0% with ln-testosterone in women, p = 9.8e-10; 38.0% in men, p = 1.4e-4). GAHT suppresses androgen-driven proteins (e.g., SPINT3 -7.90, INSL3 -5.35, EDDM3B -2.64, TEX101 -2.09 in CPA), while estrogen-responsive hepatic proteins move as under MHT (SHBG +0.28/+0.29 vs MHT +0.085 and ln-E2 +0.170; fibrinogen FGA and prekallikrein KLKB1 trend down on GAHT but rise with menopause).

5) Robustness: results are consistent across the CPA and SPIRO regimens (menopause concordance 21.7% vs 17.5%; MHT<57 66.5% vs 82.5%; MHT>=57 74.1% vs 80.0%), across correlation metrics, and in composite signatures (estrogenic signature rho = +0.122, perm p = 5.0e-4; androgenic signature within the GAHT set rho = -0.254).

Interpretation: exogenous estradiol plus androgen suppression reproduces the estrogen-REPLENT (premenopausal) protein state, whereas natural menopause reflects estrogen LOSS — the two interventions move the same proteins in opposite directions, and MHT (estrogen re-addition after menopause) moves them the same way GAHT does. Exceptions exist at the individual-protein level (e.g., leptin rises on GAHT and is also higher in menopause comparisons; CPA-specific prolactin rise).

Caveats: conclusions rest on directions/ranks/enrichments from pre-computed mixed-model summaries (no raw NPX matrix; magnitudes not comparable across comparators); GAHT arms are small (n=20) and 6 months only; MHT/menopause associations are observational and confounded by indication; Menopause>=57 (3 significant proteins) and male ln-estradiol (0) were unpowered and excluded; estrogen effects cannot be separated from gonadotropin (FSH/LH) or aging effects with these tables.
da-13-6.notes: The agent performed a rigorous, reproducible analysis with correct data preparation, matching, and biological interpretation, but fell short on per-regimen concordance quantification and missed key discordant proteins (CXCL13, NOS3) and detailed regimen-difference interpretation, resulting in B for criteria 3, 4, and 5.

da-14-1.answer:
Clustering of the 22 sepsis endotyping signature scores (3,948 patients, 10 cohorts) by pairwise Pearson correlation (distance = 1 - r, average linkage, cut at d = 0.85; bootstrap B = 200 and leave-one-cohort-out validated) yields four clusters plus one bridge signature:

CLUSTER 1 - Immunoprotective / adaptive axis (mean within-cluster r = 0.74; bootstrap same-cluster frequency = 1.00; every member independently correlates with LOWER 30-day mortality, r = -0.13 to -0.20):
  adaptive_score (Sweeney adaptive), yao_IA_score (Yao immunoadaptive; r with adaptive = 0.86), mars3_score, mod4_score, protective_score (mod3+mod4).

CLUSTER 2 - Wong severity / alternative-inflammation block (weakest, provisional; mean within-cluster r = 0.29; bootstrap PAC = 0.77):
  wong_score, mars4_score, mod3_score. The Wong score is the most isolated signature in the full cohort (max |r| = 0.26); in sepsis-only patients it merges into the inflammatory cluster, so this block is cohort-sensitive and should be treated as tentative.

CLUSTER 3 - Hyperinflammatory / myeloid-lymphoid dysregulation / SRS2 axis (dominant cluster; mean within-cluster r = 0.47; bootstrap PAC = 1.00 for the 9-signature core; every member correlates with HIGHER 30-day mortality, r = 0.11 to 0.19):
  inflammopathic_score (Sweeney), yao_IN_score, davenport_SRSq and cano_SRSq (the two SRS implementations are nearly identical, r = 0.89), mars2_score, mod1_score, mod2_score, detrimental_score (= mod1+mod2), myeloid_score, lymphoid_score, som_score (detrimental/protective ratio).

CLUSTER 4 - Interferon/monocyte sub-axis (mean within-cluster r = 0.76; bootstrap PAC = 1.00; reproduced in all cohort holdouts):
  yao_IC_score, mars1_score. A cohesive monocyte/interferon-related program, positively correlated with the myeloid-dysregulation arm of Cluster 3 (mars1~myeloid r = 0.48, mars1~som r = 0.38) but anti-correlated with the Cluster-1 protective axis (mars1~adaptive r = -0.46); yao_IC~yao_IN is negative (-0.27), i.e., the two Yao subtypes are mutually exclusive patient states.

BRIDGE SIGNATURE:
  coagulopathic_score (Sweeney) sits between Cluster 3 (r = 0.45 with inflammopathic, 0.47 with davenport_SRSq, 0.55 with som) and Cluster 2 (mars4 r = 0.13, wong r = 0.17); it joins Cluster 3 at the 0.85 cut but splits from it on stricter cuts, reflecting its partly independent coagulopathy biology.

Key numbers: strongest positive pairs - davenport_SRSq ~ cano_SRSq r = 0.888, mod1 ~ detrimental r = 0.873, mod4 ~ protective r = 0.871, adaptive ~ yao_IA r = 0.858; strongest anticorrelations - mod4 ~ lymphoid r = -0.957, adaptive ~ som r = -0.846, inflammopathic ~ adaptive r = -0.830; inflammation-axis anchors - inflammopathic ~ cano_SRSq r = 0.62 (0.66 sepsis-only), davenport_SRSq ~ som r = 0.81, inflammopathic ~ yao_IN r = 0.53. Cophenetic correlation of the tree = 0.891; the Cluster-1 and Cluster-4 memberships reproduce exactly when any of the 6 cohorts is held out, and in a sepsis-only (n = 1,928 baseline) sensitivity analysis Cluster 1 is identical while the Wong/mars4/mod3 block merges into the hyperinflammatory cluster.

Bottom line: the published sepsis endotyping schemes do not behave as independent classifiers. They collapse into ~3-4 consensus axes: (1) a protective/adaptive axis (Sweeney-adaptive, Yao-IA, MARS3, protective subspaces), (2) a hyperinflammatory/SRS2/myeloid-lymphoid dysregulation axis (Sweeney-inflammopathic, Yao-IN, both SRSq scores, MARS2, detrimental subspaces) that carries the mortality signal, (3) a Yao-IC/MARS1 interferon-monocyte sub-axis, and (4) a weak, provisional Wong/mars4/mod3 block, with Sweeney-coagulopathic as a bridge between the inflammatory and coagulation-severity ends.
da-14-1.notes: The analysis is thorough and methodologically sound, with a minor shortcoming in correlation methodology where Pearson was primary and Spearman only a sensitivity check, preventing full marks on criterion 2.

da-14-3.answer:
Among critically ill (ICU) patients with infection sampled at baseline (admission), one observation per patient (n = 2,203 unique patients; cohort flow: 3,948 samples -> 2,892 infected samples -> 2,214 baseline -> 2,203 patients), the proportions in the four immune dysregulation subgroups are:

1. System-wide (both myeloid- and lymphoid-lineage dysregulation): 961 patients = 43.6% (95% CI 41.5-45.7%)
2. Lymphoid dysregulation: 582 patients = 26.4% (95% CI 24.6-28.3%)
3. Balanced (neither lineage axis dysregulated): 548 patients = 24.9% (95% CI 23.1-26.7%)
4. Myeloid dysregulation: 112 patients = 5.1% (95% CI 4.2-6.0%)

Summary: roughly 44% of critically ill patients fall into the system-wide subgroup, ~26% into lymphoid dysregulation, ~25% are balanced, and only ~5% show isolated myeloid dysregulation; ~75% of patients show dysregulation of at least one lineage axis. These proportions are robust to including non-infected (SIRS-like) ICU patients (43.3% / 26.5% / 24.8% / 5.4%; n = 2,424). The system-wide subgroup is the most severe (62.7% of severe vs 23.6% of non-severe patients; chi-square p ~ 1e-94), has the highest 30-day mortality (19.1%; odds ratio 2.69 vs all other subgroups), and concords strongly with the published Sweeney inflammopathic/coagulopathic and Davenport SRS1 endotypes; the balanced subgroup is predominantly Sweeney-adaptive/SRS3 with the lowest mortality (5.2%).

Primary answer (one line): system-wide 43.6%, lymphoid dysregulation 26.4%, balanced 24.9%, myeloid dysregulation 5.1% of critically ill patients.
da-14-3.notes: The agent fully addresses the analysis goal with rigorous data handling, explicit subgroup threshold logic, exact proportion reporting, clear interpretation with limitations, and sourced references.

da-14-8.answer:
Yes. Both gene sets are strongly and positively correlated within themselves across the 3,948 patients, far above the correlation shown by random gene sets of the same size drawn from the same 201-gene panel.

Myeloid detrimental genes (25 genes inferred from |r| with myeloid_detrimental_score; r = 0.53-0.84): LTF, CEACAM8, OLFM4, LCN2, CTSG, ARG1, DEFA4, CAMP, CD24, S100A12, TXN, ANXA3, AZU1, NQO2, ORM1, BCL6, UBAP1, MAPK14, STOM, ITGAM, ARPC5, GADD45A, KLHL2, HK3, TLR8. All 300/300 pairwise Pearson correlations are positive: mean r = +0.487 (median 0.496, IQR 0.310-0.687, range 0.011-0.904); 76% of pairs exceed r = 0.3 and 49% exceed r = 0.5; PC1 explains 52.7% of the set's variance. The set contains two co-expression blocks (neutrophil granule genes mean r = 0.581; signaling/metabolic genes mean r = 0.628, cross-block 0.346).

Lymphoid protective genes (37 genes inferred from |r| with lymphoid_protective_score; r = 0.43-0.92): DYRK2, PLCG1, CD3E, CD3G, CAMK4, FYN, TTC3, ZNF831, CD247, SIDT1, TRIB2, ZAP70, CAMK2D, BUB3, MAP4K1, NOP53, BMS1, AHNAK, NAT10, UBE3A, SEMA4F, SMYD2, MDC1, EXOC2, POU2F2, NFATC1, RAPGEF1, PIK3R1, SENP5, DBT, THOC1, TP53BP1, DNAJA3, PIK3C2A, ARL14EP, HLA-DOA, ZCCHC4. All 666/666 pairwise correlations are positive: mean r = +0.658 (median 0.719, IQR 0.661-0.765, range 0.452-0.894); 100% of pairs exceed r = 0.3 and 98% exceed r = 0.5; PC1 explains 67.1% of variance (PC2 only 4.6%) - a single tightly co-regulated axis (TCR/BCR signalosome plus lymphoid competence: CD3E/CD3G/CD247/ZAP70/PLCG1/FYN/CAMK4-NFATC1, POU2F2, HLA-DOA).

Against a matched null (2,000 random gene sets of the same size from the same panel, mean within-set r = 0.150 +/- 0.03), both sets are far more internally correlated than chance: z = +10.2 for the myeloid detrimental set (0.487 vs 0.151) and z = +20.0 for the lymphoid protective set (0.658 vs 0.150); empirical p < 5e-4 each. The lymphoid protective set is significantly more internally correlated than the myeloid detrimental set (difference in mean pairwise r = +0.171, bootstrap 95% CI 0.145-0.198). Only 1 of the 966 within-set pairs (AZU1-TLR8, r = 0.011, p = 0.49) is not individually significant.

Robustness: results hold in sepsis-baseline patients only (n = 2,214; within-set mean r = 0.513 detrimental / 0.637 protective), in every individual recruitment site separately (10/10 sites positive; ranges 0.250-0.608 and 0.416-0.763), after regressing site/batch dummies out of genes and scores (0.412 / 0.562), and using Spearman rank correlation (0.468 / 0.705). The two sets are negatively correlated with each other (mean cross-set pairwise r = -0.337; parent scores r = -0.400), consistent with the myeloid-inflammatory (neutrophil activation/degranulation, emergency granulopoiesis) and lymphoid-protective (lymphocyte antigen-receptor signaling competence) programs behaving as opposite poles of one sepsis immune-state axis.

Caveat: gene-set membership was not provided and was inferred from the score-gene correlations (validated: disjoint sets, competitive enrichment p = 5e-5, score vs set-mean-expression r = 0.92-0.98); borderline genes could differ from the true underlying lists without changing the conclusion. Bulk whole-blood expression cannot separate cell-composition shifts from per-cell co-regulation as the source of the correlation.
da-14-8.notes: The agent correctly recovered and analyzed gene sets, computed within-set correlations, and provided robust biological interpretation, but it did not perform the low-coherence gene identification required by the rubric and omitted some bias/threshold limitations.

da-15-2.answer:
Yes — WGCNA identifies coordinated, dysregulated gene programs in ALS spinal cord, and they replicate across all three tissue levels.

WHAT WAS DONE
Signed WGCNA networks were built separately from raw counts for cervical (174 samples, 22,284 genes), lumbar (151, 22,394) and thoracic (52, 22,050) spinal cord: DESeq2-VST normalization; tissue-specific soft powers (12, 7, 10; scale-free R2 >= 0.80); TOM clustering with dynamic tree cut + module merging (27/23/33 modules). Module eigengenes were related to ALS status by OLS adjusted for age, sex, RIN, library-prep batch and 5 genotype PCs (ALS-AD/ALS-FTD codes and covariate-missing samples excluded).

MAIN FINDINGS
1) A microglial/immune program is UP in ALS in every level: cervical ME63 (beta +0.113, q 1.9e-16), lumbar ME17 (+0.092, q 3.1e-7), thoracic ME29 (+0.171, q 0.017). These modules are microglia-enriched (Mathys markers, fold-enrichment 10.8-16.2, q <= 1e-12), carry GO terms for MHC-II antigen presentation, leukocyte-mediated immunity and adaptive immune response (q <= 1e-16), and their hubs are HAVCR2, CD68, CTSS, C3AR1, SPI1, PTPN6, VAV1, BTK. Top genes driving the signal (GPNMB +2.8 logFC, LYZ, APOE, APOC1, CTSS, ACP5, ASAH1) match the disease-associated-microglia program. The same modules are stronger in short-duration donors (duration q 1.9e-5 cervical, 1.2e-4 thoracic), i.e. activation tracks fast progression. A lumbar T-cell module (CD3E, CD8A, LCK, CCL5) is also up (q 0.016).
2) Oligodendrocyte/myelin programs are DOWN in ALS: cervical ME51 (beta -0.106, q 1.9e-16) and ME17 (-0.086, q 4.1e-9), lumbar ME14 (-0.103, q 1.5e-9) and ME21 (-0.094, q 6.2e-10), thoracic ME4 (-0.190, q 0.012). Hubs PLP1, MAG, MOG, MYRF, CNP, ERMN; GO: myelination, axon ensheathment, oligodendrocyte differentiation. Consistent with demyelination in affected cord levels.
3) Neuronal/synaptic modules are DOWN (cervical ME5, hubs SYN1, DNM1, SVOP, CELF4; GO "modulation of chemical synaptic transmission" q 8.4e-50), and astrocyte modules are UP (cervical ME14 q 5.5e-9; thoracic ME26 q 0.019; hubs AQP4, NFIA), consistent with motor-neuron loss and reactive astrogliosis.
4) The programs are real and reproducible: all tested modules are preserved across tissue levels (connectivity Spearman rho 0.47-0.97, permutation q < 0.05 in 76/77 tests), and 19/21 (90.5%) cross-tissue module matches with two-sided significance show concordant ALS direction.

CAVEATS
Bulk RNA-seq modules indicate cell-type-associated programs (cortical snRNAseq markers), not proof of cell identity; post-mortem confounding (RIN, agonal state, medication) is adjusted but not fully removable; thoracic power is limited (n = 52); the Oeckl CSF/spinal-cord proteomics dataset named in the task is not present in the data directory, so protein-level validation could not be performed.

CONCLUSION
WGCNA robustly resolves the known ALS glial signature as coordinated module-level programs — microglial/immune activation up, oligodendrocyte-myelin and neuronal-synaptic programs down — reproducible across cervical, lumbar and thoracic cord, with candidate hub genes (HAVCR2, CD68, SPI1, AQP4 vs PLP1, MAG, MYRF, SYN1) nominating regulators for follow-up.
da-15-2.notes: The analysis is technically sound and well-documented, with correct WGCNA implementation and thorough enrichment reporting, but it failed to restrict network construction to ALS samples only as required, and batch correction on the expression data was incomplete.

da-16-1.answer:
Question: Can unsupervised clustering of hepatic transcriptomes (GSE135251, 206 NAFLD biopsies) stratify patients by disease severity for clinical-trial enrichment?

ANSWER: No. Unsupervised clustering of the hepatic transcriptomes does NOT stratify NAFLD patients by disease severity. The cohort contains a statistically robust binary molecular partition, but its clusters are clinically indistinguishable, and the dominant variance in the data is technical rather than biological.

WHAT WAS DONE
- Metadata from the GEO series matrix: 216 samples = 206 NAFLD cases (NAFL 51, NASH_F0-F1 34, NASH_F2 53, NASH_F3 54, NASH_F4 14) + 10 healthy controls; fibrosis stage 0-4, NAS 0-8, early (F0-F2, n=138) vs moderate (F3-F4, n=68); no missing values. Controls were excluded before clustering.
- Counts: 216 HTSeq files, 5 __-summary rows dropped per file -> 64,253 genes; filtered to 13,729 genes (CPM > 1 in >=30% of samples); TMM normalization (edgeR 4.0.16); log2-CPM (prior count 2).
- PCA + Ward hierarchical clustering on PC scores of the 206 NAFLD cases, k=2..8 assessed by mean silhouette, with sensitivity analyses (top-5,000-MAD genes, PC1-3, gene-scaled PCA, k up to 4, technical-covariate removal).

KEY RESULTS
1. The primary solution (all genes, PC1-2, Ward, k=2) splits the cohort 50 vs 156 with real structure: silhouette 0.472, cophenetic r=0.729, permutation test of silhouette p=0.0005, bootstrap within/between co-clustering 0.864/0.130, 0.71-0.94 agreement with alternative feature spaces.
2. But the clusters do NOT differ by any severity feature (chi-square / Fisher exact / Kruskal-Wallis / Spearman):
   - Fibrosis stage 0-4: chi2=3.88, dof=4, p=0.422 (medians 2 vs 2, p=0.725)
   - Advanced fibrosis F3-F4: 32.0% vs 33.3%, Fisher p=1.000
   - NAS score: medians 5 vs 5 (means 4.22 vs 4.61), Kruskal-Wallis p=0.225
   - NASH group (NAFL to NASH_F4): chi2=3.28, dof=4, p=0.512
   - Early vs moderate: 68.0% vs 66.7% early, chi2 p=0.999
   - All 28 tests across the sensitivity grid (feature spaces x PC number x k) were non-significant; smallest p anywhere = 0.178.
3. What the clusters actually track (exploratory): the file-name sequencing-batch proxy (chi2=12.06, p=0.0072; all 3 minority-site samples in the small cluster) and library size (Spearman rho=0.374, p<1e-7). PC1 correlates with library size (rho=-0.471, p=9.4e-13) but not fibrosis (rho=0.059) or NAS (rho=-0.078). As a positive control, re-clustering all 216 samples did not cleanly separate the 10 healthy controls from NAFLD cases either - further evidence that variance is dominated by technical factors.
4. Severity signal exists but is continuous, not discrete: after regressing out library size and batch, residual PC3 correlates strongly with fibrosis (rho=0.638, p=6.6e-25) and NAS (rho=0.467, p=1.6e-12), yet even there no Ward partition (k=2-4, 2-4 PCs) yields consistently significant severity-separated clusters (silhouettes <=0.36, non-replicating p~0.02-0.03).

INTERPRETATION AND IMPLICATION FOR TRIAL ENRICHMENT
Hepatic transcriptomic variation across the NAFLD spectrum in GSE135251 forms a stable binary partition driven by sequencing/processing characteristics, not histologic severity. Fibrosis stage and NAS are encoded in the residual transcriptome as a graded (continuous) signal consistent with the known continuous histologic progression of NAFLD, but they do not define discrete unsupervised molecular subtypes in this dataset. Unsupervised whole-transcriptome clustering is therefore NOT a usable enrichment/stratification tool here; trial enrichment should instead use histologic staging (e.g., F3-F4) or supervised transcriptomic classifiers built against the severity outcome.

MAIN LIMITATIONS
- GEO provides no explicit batch, sex, age, or BMI fields; the batch proxy derives from file-naming conventions, so residual site effects within the largest naming group cannot be excluded.
- Bulk-tissue signal may dilute severity-relevant cell-type changes; genes were analyzed by Ensembl ID without external annotation.
- Early/moderate and NASH-group labels are deterministic re-codings of fibrosis stage in this cohort, so their tests are not independent of the fibrosis test.
- Controls (n=10, healthy liver) are too few for the positive control to be definitive.

PIPELINE SUMMARY: 216 files -> 216 samples (206 NAFLD analyzed) -> 64,253 genes -> 13,729 after filtering -> TMM log2-CPM -> PCA (PC1 28.4%, PC2 9.7% var) -> Ward k=2 (50 vs 156, silhouette 0.472) -> all severity tests null (p >= 0.178 across 28 specifications).
da-16-1.notes: The agent performed a rigorous and technically sound analysis; the only rubric deduction is for not applying a formal multiple-testing correction in criterion 5, while all other criteria meet the A-level standard.

da-17-1.answer:
Question: Which circulating immune cell populations show significantly altered frequencies in SLE patients compared to healthy controls?

Answer (based on 1,263,676 PBMCs from 274 samples: 175 SLE draws from 162 donors vs 99 healthy-control draws, tested at the sample level with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR control):

SIX POPULATIONS ARE SIGNIFICANTLY ALTERED IN SLE (FDR q < 0.05, robust to batch, age, sex, ethnicity and donor-overlap sensitivity checks):

INCREASED in SLE:
1. Classical monocytes (CD14++): 26.2% of PBMCs (median) in SLE vs 17.7% in controls; +10.7 percentage points (weighted); log2 fold-change +0.73; Wilcoxon p = 2.1e-13, q = 1.1e-12.
2. Non-classical monocytes (CD14+CD16++): 3.9% vs 2.8%; +1.2 pp; log2FC +0.46; p = 7.5e-05, q = 1.7e-04.
3. Proliferating (Ki-67/cycling) lymphocytes: 0.65% vs 0.36%; +0.4 pp; log2FC +0.81; p = 1.9e-10, q = 5.3e-10.

DECREASED in SLE:
4. CD4-positive alpha-beta T cells (total): 23.2% vs 37.4%; -12.9 pp; log2FC -0.98; p = 3.4e-19, q = 3.8e-18 (the single most significant alteration in the cohort). At fine-grained resolution this is a naive CD4 T-cell loss (16.5% vs 33.9%, -16.0 pp, q = 6.4e-23) with compensatory expansion of effector-memory CD4 T cells (+4.3 pp, q = 1.6e-11) and regulatory CD4 T cells (+1.8 pp, q = 1.1e-13).
5. Plasmacytoid dendritic cells: 0.24% vs 0.51%; -0.3 pp; log2FC -1.07 (largest relative decrease among DC subsets); p = 3.9e-12, q = 1.4e-11.
6. Conventional dendritic cells: 1.15% vs 1.48%; -0.2 pp; log2FC -0.37; p = 4.0e-04, q = 7.4e-04.

ALSO ALTERED at fine-grained resolution (all q < 0.05, among the 14 annotated lymphoid populations): MAIT T cells strongly decreased (0.50% vs 2.10%, log2FC -2.03, q = 1.4e-17); memory B cells decreased (3.3% vs 5.3%, -2.6 pp, q = 9.9e-11); GZMH+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes increased (10.5% vs 4.9%, +7.9 pp, q = 3.8e-07); GZMK+ cytotoxic T cells increased (+2.6 pp, q = 1.7e-04); atypical/double-negative B cells increased (0.40% vs 0.28%, q = 5.9e-04); naive B cells increased (11.6% vs 9.7%, +4.4 pp, q = 4.7e-02); progenitors decreased (q = 7.2e-05).

NOT SIGNIFICANTLY ALTERED (candidates to exclude): CD8+ alpha-beta T cells (+2.4 pp, q = 0.15; rises only in active disease), NK cells (q = 0.10; borderline decrease, batch-sensitive), plasmablasts (q = 0.71; elevated only in the small flare subset), and naive CD8 T cells (q = 0.24). Borderline/modest: B cells (total, -0.5 pp, q = 0.045 in the primary test but sensitive to batch/donor handling).

KEY STATISTICS: the six core alterations persist in every sensitivity analysis performed - compositional (CLR) re-testing (worst-case q = 0.0063), processing-cohort-stratified Wilcoxon (q = 0.0147), covariate-adjusted regression on age + sex + ethnicity + cohort (q = 0.0210), donor-level deduplication to one sample per donor (q = 0.0072), and the managed-disease-only subgroup (q < 1e-4, so the signature is not flare-driven). The naive CD4 T-cell deficit does not correlate with donor age in controls (r = +0.17) and persists across the whole 20-80-year age range, so it is disease-linked rather than age-linked. As a diagnostic panel, the 11 population frequencies classify SLE vs control at 5-fold cross-validated AUC 0.92 (best single marker: CD4 T-cell frequency, AUC 0.82).

BIOLOGICAL INTERPRETATION: SLE shows a coordinated myeloid/interferon-axis shift - expanded classical and non-classical monocytes together with depleted blood pDC (the "pDC paradox" of IFN-driven tissue homing), a naive-to-effector CD4 T-cell reconfiguration with expanded Tregs, contracted memory B cells with expanded naive/atypical B cells, MAIT lymphopenia, and expanded cytotoxic GZMH+ and proliferating lymphocytes.

CAVEATS: single-cell data give relative composition only (absolute counts unavailable, so concurrent lymphopenia cannot be separated from true myeloid expansion); 146/175 SLE samples were on therapy ("managed"), so treatment effects cannot be excluded; the fine (ct_cov) annotation is missing for all monocytes/DCs, limiting that panel to lymphoid subsets; and the AUC is cross-validated within this cohort, not externally validated.

Methods in brief: per-sample cell-type frequencies from raw counts (274 samples x 11 populations; 200-cell minimum per sample); two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests SLE vs control with permutation calibration (9,999 permutations); effect sizes as log2 fold-change of group-median Haldane-Anscombe-adjusted frequencies; BH FDR per annotation level; full details and code in trace.md.
da-17-1.notes: The analysis is robust with appropriate statistical methods and clear reporting, but it uses sample-level rather than donor-level aggregation and fails to identify three of the eight expected significant cell types, leading to partial credit on criteria 2,3,5.

  ATP2B1, MS4A1, BLK, and lncRNAs (SNHG9, LINC00910).

EVIDENCE THAT THE UP-PROGRAM IS TYPE-I IFN DRIVEN
1. Of the provided 25-gene type-I ISG signature, 12 genes are measurable in this
   dataset (13, e.g. OAS1/2/3, MX1, SIGLEC1, RSAD2, EPSTI1, were author-filtered
   from the delivered gene universe). All 12 are up-regulated; mean log2FC +2.28
   vs +0.26 genome-wide background; CAMERA set-level test within the same model:
   Direction = Up, P = 2.8e-29.
2. Donor-level ISG score (mean log1p-CP10k of the 12 genes) separates every SLE
   group from controls: control 0.37 (n=99) < managed 0.97 (n=144) < flare 1.21
   (n=12) < treated 1.59 (n=6); Kruskal-Wallis p = 9.3e-21; SLE-vs-control
   Mann-Whitney AUC = 0.85.
3. Independent per-cell Wilcoxon cross-check (306,745 cells, donor-level
   normalization) agrees on direction: 148/280 edgeR-up genes also up per cell
   (45.6x enriched over chance); 189/191 edgeR-down genes also down; Spearman
   rho(edgeR logFC, Wilcoxon score) = 0.46. Per-cell top up-genes are the same
   ISGs (IFI6, IFITM3, IFI44L, ISG15, LY6E, IFI44, IFI27, IFIT3...).
4. The same IFN program appears in non-classical monocytes (252 FDR genes;
   top: ISG15, IFI27, IFI6, STAT1, IFI44L) and conventional DCs (112 FDR genes;
   top: IFI6, IFI44L, ISG15, IFITM3, IFI27), and a flare-vs-control contrast
   (n=12 flare donors) recapitulates it (IFI27 +4.37, CXCL10 +3.12, IFIT3 +2.33).

   genes; restricting to females (147 SLE / 97 controls) keeps 440/471; all 12
   signature genes remain up in both sensitivity runs.

INTERPRETATION
SLE classical monocytes are locked in a constitutive type-I interferon state:
up-regulation of the IFNAR -> JAK1/TYK2 -> STAT1/STAT2 -> IRF7 axis and its
antiviral/antiproliferative effectors (IFIT/IFI/ISG15/HERC5/APOBEC3A families),
plus the IFN-induced chemokine CXCL10 that can recruit CXCR3+ pDC and T cells and
sustain the loop. Simultaneously, AP-1 factors (FOS, JUND) and core monocyte
identity/antigen-presentation genes are down-regulated, consistent with IFN-driven
reprogramming of monocyte effector function. Therapeutically, the IFN pathway is
directly druggable and is the target of approved SLE biologics (anifrolumab,
anti-IFNAR1; refs: Furie NEJM 2019, Morand NEJM 2020), with CXCL10/CXCR3 and BAFF
(TNFSF13B) axes as additional druggable nodes.

CAVEATS
Genes were tested within the 1,889 author-retained gene universe (13/25 signature
genes unmeasurable); Processing_Cohort 1 contains only controls (cohort adjusted,
93% of findings robust to covariate choice); "treated" n=6 limits severity claims;
observational design - no causal ordering between IFN signaling, medication
exposure, and monocyte dysfunction.
