da-18-1.answer:
GENOMIC LANDSCAPE OF BREAST CANCER RECEPTOR SUBTYPES
Cohort: MSK-IMPACT targeted-panel profiling, 1,803 samples from 1,649 patients (HR+/HER2- 1,422; HR+/HER2+ 141; HR-/HER2+ 66; TNBC 174), from data_clinical_sample.txt (1,918 samples; 115 excluded for unknown/equivocal receptor status), data_mutations.txt (9,314 MAF rows, 9,268 nonsynonymous) and data_cna.txt (474 genes; only deep-deletion -2 and amplification +2 calls present).

HOW THE LANDSCAPES DIFFER

1) TP53 defines a graded loss-of-function axis. Mutation frequency rises monotonically from HR+/HER2- 26.8% (381/1,422) to HR+/HER2+ 45.4% (64/141), HR-/HER2+ 78.8% (52/66) and TNBC 89.7% (156/174); overall association chi-square q = 5e-68. Truncating TP53 lesions are most frequent in TNBC (56% of mutated tumors vs 37% in HR+/HER2-). TP53 is the near-universal lesion of triple-negative and HER2-enriched disease.

2) PI3K-pathway alterations define HR+ disease and invert in TNBC. PIK3CA: 41.1% HR+/HER2-, 38.3% HR+/HER2+, 25.8% HR-/HER2+, 14.4% TNBC (OR = 0.24, TNBC vs HR+/HER2-, p = 4e-13; hotspots p.H1047R/L, p.E545K, p.E542K in all subtypes). PIK3R1 shows the opposite polarity (1.3% HR+/HER2- vs 7.5% TNBC, q = 1.7e-5), and AKT1 p.E17K is almost confined to HR+/HER2- (6.3%). PTEN inactivation (mutation or deep deletion) is most common in TNBC (14.9%; deep deletion OR = 3.1, p = 0.007). Any PI3K-pathway alteration: 54% HR+/HER2-, 45% HR+/HER2+, 33% HR-/HER2+ and TNBC.

3) GATA3 is a binary luminal marker: 17.5% (HR+/HER2-) and 17.0% (HR+/HER2+) vs 0 of 240 HR- tumors (Fisher p = 5.5e-19). Similarly MAP3K1 (9.0% HR+/HER2- vs 1.5-2.9% elsewhere), MAP2K4 (4.0%), AKT1 and the 11q13 (CCND1 21.1%, FGF19/FGF3/FGF4) and 8p11-12 (FGFR1 13.2%, PAK1 11.4%) amplifications mark HR+ (especially HR+/HER2-) tumors. CDH1 mutation (18.7% in HR+/HER2-) is histology-driven: 81% of lobular vs 2.0% of ductal HR+/HER2- tumors (OR = 210.6, p = 8e-169).

4) ERBB2/17q12 amplification is the genomic definition of the HER2+ arms: 66.7% of HR+/HER2+ and 86.4% of HR-/HER2+ samples vs 1.5% of HR+/HER2- and 0.6% of TNBC (OR 40.1 and 88.5, q = 2.6e-236). CDK12 is co-amplified with ERBB2 in 117/117 cases; RARA (19.1%), SPOP (13.5%) and HOXB13 amps tag the same 17q amplicon. Notably 1.5% of clinically HR+/HER2- tumors harbor ERBB2 amplification and 4.4% carry ERBB2 mutations - ERBB2-actionable subcohorts within receptor-negative-by-IHC disease. HER2+ tumors are also amplification-rich overall (mean 0.9-1.0% of panel genes amplified vs 0.5-0.6% in HR+/HER2-/TNBC, KW p = 1.4e-18) and more TP53-mutant.

5) TNBC has a distinct DNA-repair and amplicon profile: RB1 inactivation (mutation or deep deletion) 16.1% (deep deletion OR = 9.9, q = 2.3e-8), BRCA1/2 or PALB2 mutation 8.6% and any homologous-repair gene mutation 11.5% (the PARP-inhibitor subcohort), MYC amplification 15.5%, plus TNBC-restricted focal amplicons CCND2 (12p13, OR = 78.5), KDM5A, RAD52 and CCNE1 (19q12, 5.7%; all 10 CCNE1-amplified TNBC are TP53-mutant). MAP2K4 deep deletions, by contrast, are restricted to HR+ tumors (2.1%).

6) ESR1 ligand-binding-domain mutations (Y537S/C/N, D538G - 130 of 175 ESR1 mutations) occur only in HR+ tumors (8.5-9.9%) and are 11-fold enriched in metastases vs treatment-naive primaries (15.0% vs 1.6%, OR = 11.1, p = 6e-23) - the genomic signature of endocrine-therapy exposure and acquired resistance. ESR1-mutant tumors are TP53-wild-type-enriched (OR = 0.39), marking a lower-grade luminal subgroup.

7) Mutation burden is low in all groups (median 3-4 nonsynonymous mutations/sample on the ~1.1 Mb panel; the provided TMB column is mis-scaled by a factor of 30 - counts/30 - and was recomputed). Medians: HR+/HER2- 3, HR+/HER2+ 3, HR-/HER2+ 4, TNBC 4; the overall difference is not significant (Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.085) and pairwise differences (TNBC and HR+/HER2+ vs HR+/HER2-, p = 0.014/0.042 unadjusted) do not survive correction - burden differences across subtypes are modest within this panel; the sole hypermutant (445 mutations) is an MSH2/MSH6/POLD1/POLE-mutant outlier.

ACTIONABLE SUBCOHORTS WITHIN RECEPTOR GROUPS (frequencies)
- PIK3CA mutation (alpelisib + endocrine): 41.1% HR+/HER2-, 38.3% HR+/HER2+, 25.8% HR-/HER2+, 14.4% TNBC.
- ERBB2 amplification (HER2-directed therapy): 86.4% HR-/HER2+, 66.7% HR+/HER2+, 1.5% HR+/HER2-, 0.6% TNBC; 21-22% of HER2+ tumors are also PIK3CA-mutant (co-targeting decisions).
- ESR1 mutation (elacestrant): ~8.5-9.9% of HR+ tumors (15% of HR+ metastases), 0% HR-.
- BRCA1/2/PALB2 (PARP inhibitors): 4.9-8.6% across subtypes, highest in TNBC (8.6%); any HRR-gene mutation 6-12%.
- PTEN loss (AKT inhibition): highest in TNBC (14.9%).
- CDK4/6-axis amplification (CCND1 or FGFR1): 29.2% HR+/HER2-, 26.2% HR+/HER2+, 12.1% HR-/HER2+, 8.0% TNBC.

BOTTOM LINE: HR+ tumors are PI3K/GATA3/ER-axis and 11q13/8p11 amplification driven with lobular CDH1 lesions and acquired ESR1-LBD mutations after endocrine therapy; HER2+ tumors (either HR background) are defined by 17q12 (ERBB2/CDK12) amplification on a TP53-mutant, amplification-rich background; TNBC is defined by near-universal TP53 loss-of-function plus RB1/PTEN inactivation, MYC/CCNE1/CCND2 amplification, and the highest homologous-repair-lesion load. Clinically, receptor status and genotype are complementary: every receptor group contains actionable subcohorts, most notably ERBB2 amplification in 1.5% of HR+/HER2- tumors, PIK3CA mutations in 14% of TNBC, and HRR lesions in 9-12% of every subtype.

LIMITATIONS: cross-sectional design (no treatment-response or survival data; "acquired" ESR1 inference rests on naive-primary vs metastatic comparison); targeted panel (no genome-wide CNA, signatures, or structural variants; gene-level +/-2 calls only, so amplicon membership is inferred); somatic variants only (germline BRCA1/2 carriers undercounted, so HRR fractions are lower bounds); small HR-/HER2+ arm (n = 66) gives low power; several small-gene signals (RHOA, PRDM1, PTPN11, CD79A, TGFBR1) are nominal; 154 patients contribute >1 sample; 6.8% of samples show primary-vs-sequenced-sample receptor discordance, blurring subtype boundaries.

Method summary: subtypes from RECEPTOR_STATUS_PRIMARY; nonsynonymous MAF rows collapsed to a binary gene-by-sample matrix (446 genes x 1,803 samples); CNA +/-2 calls aligned to the same samples; 4-group chi-square per gene with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR, pairwise Fisher exact with odds ratios; Kruskal-Wallis/Mann-Whitney for burden; full trace with code in trace.md; tables in analysis/, figures in figures/.
da-18-1.notes: The agent performed a comprehensive and largely rigorous analysis, excelling in data integration, subtype classification, driver-gene identification, interpretation, and source reliability; minor omissions in TMB IQR reporting and ERBB2 point-mutation stratification by subtype prevent full marks in those areas.

da-18-5.answer: Cumulative frequency of MAPK pathway alterations in post-hormonal-therapy HR+/HER2- breast cancers (this dataset, n=653 post-therapy samples = metastatic biopsies + post-treatment primaries): 102/653 = 15.6% with at least one alteration in the core MAPK pathway (KRAS, NRAS, HRAS, RIT1, BRAF, ARAF, RAF1, MAP2K1, MAP2K2, MAPK1, MAPK3, SOS1, SHOC2, PTPN11 mutations/amplifications; NF1, RASA1, SPRED1 mutations/deep deletions), versus 46/657 = 7.0% in treatment-naive primary HR+/HER2- tumors (Fisher exact p = 8.1e-07, OR 2.46, 95% CI 1.70-3.52). Sensitivity: post-treatment primaries alone 6/40 = 15.0%; post-treatment + post-neoadjuvant primaries 11/76 = 14.5%; all non-naive samples 107/689 = 15.5%; including ERBB-family RTKs (EGFR/ERBB2/ERBB3) 22.7% post vs 12.9% naive; broadest definition (adding MAP3K1/13/14, RRAS/RRAS2, DUSP4, ERF) 29.2% post vs 23.1% naive. The post-therapy enrichment is driven mainly by NF1 loss (5.5% vs 1.8%), RIT1 mutations (2.1% vs 0.6%) and KRAS mutations (1.7% vs 0.9%), consistent with MAPK pathway activation as a mechanism of acquired endocrine resistance.
da-18-5.notes: The agent performed a rigorous HR+/HER2- cohort analysis with clear therapy classification, MAPK gene sets, union alteration counts, and enrichment testing, but missed all ESR1-related requirements, including ESR1-wild-type frequencies and mutual exclusivity testing, and its primary gene set omitted RTK genes mandated by the rubric.

da-18-7.answer:
VERDICT: Trend toward mutual exclusivity, but NOT statistically significant in the primary test. ESR1 mutations and MAPK-pathway alterations are best described as largely independent with a sub-expected overlap (leaning exclusive), and they are certainly NOT co-occurring.

PRIMARY ANALYSIS (n = 705 post-hormonal-therapy HR+/HER2- samples, 656 patients; HR_STATUS=Positive, OVERALL_HER2_STATUS=Negative, sample site != Treatment Naive Primary):
- ESR1 altered (non-synonymous mutation): 131/705 (18.6%)
- MAPK altered (non-synonymous mutation in KRAS/NRAS/HRAS/BRAF/RAF1/ARAF/MAP2K1/MAP2K2/MAPK1/MAPK3/MAP3K1/NF1/RASA1, or copy-number gain of these genes): 135/705 (19.1%)
- Tumors with BOTH: 19 observed vs 25.1 expected under independence (deficit to 76% of expectation)
- Fisher's exact test: odds ratio = 0.67 (95% CI 0.40-1.13), two-sided p = 0.14; one-sided (exclusivity) p = 0.08; permutation (20,000 draws) p = 0.083
- => Co-occurrence is sub-expected but the deficit does not reach significance; the 95% CI includes 1.0.

SENSITIVITY ANALYSES (consistent direction throughout):
- MAPK inactivation-type events only (MAP3K1/NF1/RASA1 mutation or deep deletion): 13 vs 20.1 expected, OR 0.56, p = 0.060
- MAPK activation-type events only (RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK mutation or RTK/MAPK amplification >= 2): 26 vs 31.8 expected, OR 0.73, p = 0.21
- NF1 mutation alone: OR 0.24 (2 vs 6.9 expected), p = 0.030; MAP3K1 mutation alone: OR 0.83, p = 0.73 (no exclusivity)
- ESR1 ligand-binding-domain hotspot mutants (Y537/D538/L536; n = 107) vs MAPK inactivation-type: OR 0.46 (9 vs 16.4 expected), p = 0.029; non-LBD ESR1 mutants show no deficit (OR ~ 1.0)
- Logistic regression adjusting for log10 TMB and sample type: adjusted OR = 0.50 (beta = -0.70), p = 0.014 - ESR1-mutant tumors have higher TMB (median 0.17 vs 0.13 mut/Mb, p = 1.2e-5), which biases raw counts toward co-occurrence, so the TMB-independent trend toward exclusivity is real but modest
- Robust to: one sample per patient (n = 656, OR 0.72), excluding post-neoadjuvant primaries (n = 669, OR 0.68), metastases only (n = 629, OR 0.71)

INTERPRETATION AND LIMITATIONS:
- Genuine double-altered tumors exist (19; 2.7% of cohort), so the alterations are not strictly mutually exclusive; nor do they co-occur above chance.
- The deficit is concentrated in the mechanistically expected place: endocrine-therapy-selected ESR1 LBD-hotspot clones under-harbor MAPK pathway LOSSES (especially NF1), consistent with upstream RTK/MAPK activation and ESR1 mutation being partially alternative routes of endocrine resistance (Osborne & Schiff 2011; Arpino et al. 2008).
- Power: this cohort detects only OR <= 0.47 with 80% power; the observed OR 0.67 lies in the underpowered zone, so non-significance must not be read as independence.
- "Post-hormonal therapy" is inferred from sample site annotation (no explicit endocrine-therapy field in the clinical table); targeted panel (473 genes) misses non-panel MAPK regulators, fusions, and expression-level pathway activation; subgroup p-values are nominal (uncorrected).

BOTTOM LINE: In post-hormonal-therapy HR+HER2- tumors, ESR1 mutations and MAPK-pathway alterations are not strictly mutually exclusive and not co-occurring: they co-occur less often than expected by chance (19 vs 25.1; OR 0.67, p = 0.14), with the exclusivity trend reaching significance only after TMB adjustment (p = 0.014) or within subgroups (ESR1 LBD mutants vs NF1/MAP3K1-pathway loss, OR 0.46-0.24, p ~ 0.03). The dominant genomic pattern is largely independent acquisition with a modest, mechanism-consistent lean toward mutual exclusivity.
da-18-7.notes: The analysis is statistically rigorous and transparent, but cohort selection mixes primary/metastatic samples, the primary ESR1 arm is not restricted to LBD, and the MAPK gene set deviates from the rubric-specified definition; the interpretation lacks explicit therapeutic implications.

da-19-1.answer:
Question: Which genes are most significantly downregulated upon AI-10-49 treatment downstream of CBFbeta-SMMHC inhibition in inv(16) AML?

ANSWER: MYC (c-MYC) is the single most significantly downregulated gene upon AI-10-49 treatment of ME-1 inv(16) AML cells.

Supporting statistics for MYC (from Cuffdiff gene-level differential expression, gene_exp.diff):
- log2 fold change (AI-10-49 / DMSO) = -3.298  (approximately 9.8-fold decrease)
- FPKM: DMSO = 218.30, AI-10-49 = 22.20 (mean of 3 biological replicates each)
- Cuffdiff test statistic = -19.34 (the most negative of all 3,027 significantly downregulated genes; no other gene exceeds it)
- p-value = 5 x 10^-5 (Cuffdiff numerical floor)
- q-value (Benjamini-Hochberg FDR) = 2.06 x 10^-4

Other genes among the most significantly downregulated (all q = 2.06 x 10^-4, ranked by |test statistic|):
  1. MYC       (-3.30 log2FC, test_stat -19.34)
  2. UNG       (-2.33 log2FC, test_stat -14.55)
  3. EMILIN1   (-2.29 log2FC, test_stat -14.30)
  4. CLC       (-2.75 log2FC, test_stat -14.28)
  5. UHRF1     (-2.55 log2FC, test_stat -13.71)
  6. HPDL      (-2.69 log2FC, test_stat -13.03)
  7. RTN4R     (-2.53 log2FC, test_stat -12.65)
  8. COLGALT1  (-2.15 log2FC, test_stat -12.30)
  9. CCNE1     (-2.48 log2FC, test_stat -11.97)
 10. PRDX4     (-2.12 log2FC, test_stat -11.95)

Additional notable downregulated genes with strong evidence (q = 2.06 x 10^-4):
GFI1B (-2.02), CEBPA (-1.53), IL1B (-1.72), MAT2A (-2.24), SRM (-1.68), ZFP36L2 (-2.12), DUSP7 (-1.86), FABP5 (-1.75).

Ranking purely by magnitude of fold-change among all 3,027 significantly downregulated genes (q < 0.05), the top hits are: PLD6 (-3.46), MYC (-3.30), UBE2Q2P3 (-3.19), UBE2Q2P2 (-3.09), C1orf51 (-3.05), TMEM121 (-3.02), SH2D4A (-2.98), ITPRIPL1 (-2.94), CLDN5 (-2.87), CLC (-2.75).

Biological interpretation: The dominant transcriptional response to acute CBFbeta-SMMHC inhibition is collapse of the MYC transcriptional program. Many of the other downregulated genes (UNG, CCNE1, UHRF1, MAT2A, SRM) are canonical MYC/E2F-driven factors involved in nucleotide metabolism, cell-cycle progression, epigenetic maintenance, and one-carbon metabolism. The RUNX1 (q=0.081, NS) and CBFB (q=0.147, NS) transcripts themselves are not substantially repressed, consistent with AI-10-49 blocking the CBFbeta-SMMHC:RUNX1 protein-protein interaction rather than degrading CBF complex mRNA. In contrast, stress-response genes (JUN, SESN2, RELB, TRIB3, ASNS, BIRC3) are strongly upregulated, a pattern consistent with loss of the MYC-driven survival program and induction of apoptosis.
da-19-1.notes: The agent excelled at provenance, contrast validation, and biological interpretation, but failed to apply the required q<0.01 and log2FC<=-1 filters, leading to an incorrect top-gene ranking and MYC rank; limitations were documented without actionable next steps.

da-19-3.answer:
RUNX1 chromatin occupancy does NOT collapse upon CBFbeta-SMMHC inhibition - it massively EXPANDS and INTENSIFIES, retargeting RUNX1 to pre-existing active (H3K27ac-positive) promoter and enhancer chromatin, including de novo occupancy of the MYC promoter.

QUANTITATIVE FINDINGS (ME-1 inv(16) AML cells, DMSO vs AI-10-49 RUNX1 ChIP-seq, 1 replicate each; consensus = union-merge of per-condition MACS2 peaks, -d 100 bp; classes = overlap of consensus regions +/-100 bp with per-condition peaks; verified by two independent implementations, bedtools v2.29.1 and NumPy, with identical results):

1. Global occupancy change:
   - RUNX1 peaks called: 1,329 (DMSO) -> 9,169 (AI-10-49), a 6.9x increase.
   - Consensus regions (n=9,190) partition: 7,876 GAINED (85.7%), 1,219 SHARED (13.3%), 95 LOST (1.0%). Bound regions: 1,314 -> 9,095 (6.9x). Covered bases: 0.33 Mb -> 3.18 Mb (~10x).
   - High-confidence peaks (q>=20): 304 -> 3,643 (12x).
   - Promoter genes targeted: 455 (DMSO) -> 4,062 (AI-10-49), ~9x.
   - Sensitivity: merge distance 0/100/250 bp gives 7,947/7,876/7,743 gained and 96/95/94 lost - conclusion invariant.

2. Retained sites get STRONGER, not weaker: at the 1,219 shared regions, signal (input-normalized fold enrichment) rises at 1,136/1,219 (93.2%), median 5.48 -> 12.53 (2.3x), median q-value 12.5 -> 47.3 (Wilcoxon signed-rank p = 4.2e-189; sign test p = 4.8e-237).

3. Gained occupancy sits on pre-existing ACTIVE chromatin: 84.3% of gained regions overlap an H3K27ac peak in BOTH conditions (Fisher OR ~ 90.5, p < 1e-300; genomic H3K27ac coverage is only 2.34%, i.e. 215 overlaps expected by chance vs 6,636 observed). Gained regions are enriched for promoters vs shared (36.6% vs 27.2%, z = 6.45, p = 1.1e-10). The H3K27ac landscape is broadly stable during treatment (57,784 -> 56,277 peaks, -2.6%), so the acetylome is not being erased; RUNX1 occupancy on it is what changes.

4. MYC promoter gains RUNX1 de novo: one RUNX1 region at the MYC promoter (chr8:128,747,329-128,747,624 GRCh37, ending 56 bp upstream of the TSS) is ABSENT in DMSO (0 overlapping peaks) and PRESENT after AI-10-49 (FE 4.11, q = 5.9), on a strong active promoter (H3K27ac FE ~15 in both conditions). This is the key locus-level observation: inhibition lets RUNX1 occupy the MYC promoter, the nodal pro-survival gene whose chromatin disruption mediates AI-10-49-induced apoptosis.

5. Named gained promoter targets (AML-relevant panel): CEBPA, CEBPG, ETS2, NR4A2, FOS, EGR1, DUSP6, FLT3, BCL2, MCL1, GADD45A, MMP9, PLAUR, MYC; ITGAM is shared (strongest protein-coding site, FE 48.0). Only 95 regions are lost (37 promoter genes, e.g. CEBPE, JMJD1C, WDR24), with low DMSO signal (median FE 5.15) - loss is a minor part of the response.

INTERPRETATION: The data support a redistribution-and-retargeting model rather than simple release-from-sequestration. CBFbeta-SMMHC inhibition multiplies the number of RUNX1-occupied sites ~7-fold and strengthens occupancy at essentially all retained sites, with new binding concentrated at active regulatory elements (35.3% of all regions promoter-proximal; 90.4% of all regions H3K27ac-positive vs 2.34% genome coverage). The appearance of RUNX1 at the MYC promoter, together with gained occupancy of myeloid differentiation and apoptosis-regulatory genes (CEBPA, ETS2, NR4A2, GADD45A), provides a chromatin-level mechanism for AI-10-49's pro-apoptotic, MYC-centric therapeutic effect in inv(16) AML.

CAVEATS: single ChIP-seq replicate per condition (no replicate-level statistics; low-signal gained sites such as the MYC promoter site are the most exposed to false positives); no RNA-seq/ATAC-seq files in the workspace, so downstream expression and accessibility consequences are inferred, not computed; no ChIP for CBFbeta-SMMHC itself (the sequestration-to-retargeting interpretation is indirect); peak-to-gene assignment is TSS-proximity based; per-region fold-enrichment comparisons carry a library-size caveat (the peak-count change of 6.9x is far beyond plausible size-factor effects).

Key files: runx1_occupancy/output/tables/runx1_consensus_annotated.tsv (full 9,190-region table), table1_peak_qc.tsv, table2_runx1_class_vs_h3k27ac.tsv (Fisher tests), table4_myc_locus_regions.tsv, table6_lost_regions.tsv, table7_aml_gene_panel.tsv; figure runx1_occupancy/output/figures/fig1_runx1_occupancy_summary.png; reproducibility record runx1_occupancy/README.md.
da-19-3.notes: The agent excelled in data extraction, differential occupancy computation, quantitative reporting, mechanistic interpretation, and source reliability, but the genomic feature enrichment analysis was incomplete, covering only promoter-proximal regions instead of all four feature classes with the required precedence and Fisher exact test.

da-19-4.answer:
Question: Which genomic regions show reduced H3K27ac signal upon AI-10-49 treatment (candidate enhancers driving leukemia maintenance in inv(16) AML)?

ANSWER SUMMARY
AI-10-49 (CBFbeta-SMMHC inhibitor) treatment of ME-1 inv(16) AML cells causes a global collapse of H3K27ac at RUNX1/CBFbeta-SMMHC-dependent regulatory elements. Of 71,106 consensus H3K27ac regions tested (500 bp windows centered on union MACS2 summits from both conditions), 3,473 regions show a significant >=2-fold reduction in H3K27ac (log2FC(AI/DMSO) < -1, FDR < 0.05, edgeR exact test): 1,297 promoters and 2,175 distal enhancer candidates. Within the reduced set, H3K27ac fragments drop to ~0.31x of DMSO levels, versus 0.70x genome-wide. Reduced regions are significantly enriched for RUNX1 occupancy (distal: OR 2.25, p = 1.7e-07 vs RUNX1-DMSO peaks), while regions that GAIN acetylation are depleted of RUNX1 (OR 0.15, p = 2.1e-23), consistent with collapse of the fusion-factor enhancer program.

- HOXA9 distal element (chr7, ~27.2 Mb region): 0.36x retention (log2FC -1.06, FDR 3.1e-04).
- FLT3 promoter (chr13:28.6 Mb): 0.36x retention (log2FC -1.05, FDR 1.3e-03), RUNX1-associated.
- MYC regulatory domain (chr8:128.75 Mb): strongest window decrease chr8:128,807,181-128,807,680 (136->50 frags, log2FC -1.03, FDR 0.011); promoter-proximal chr8:128,748,437-128,748,936 (471->226, FDR 0.037); window totals 1 reduced / 4 gained at FDR<0.05.

METHOD (one line each)
- Consensus regions: MACS2 summit points (narrowPeak col 10 offset) of H3K27ac peaks (FE>=2) from DMSO (GSM2715535; 57,818 summits) and AI-10-49 (GSM2715536; 56,298), clustered within 500 bp (bedtools merge -d 500) -> 71,107 clusters, expanded to 500 bp windows.
- Counting: bedtools multicov -q 30 on the two primary BAMs (35.95 M vs 37.33 M mapped reads).
- Statistics: edgeR exactTest (edgeR 4.0.16), TMM normalization, filterByExpr (71,106 kept); unreplicated design -> common dispersion fixed at phi = 0.01 (BCV = 0.1, isogenic clonal cell line per edgeR manual guidance); sensitivity sweep phi in {0.01, 0.04, 0.16, 0.25, 0.49} -> FDR<0.05 counts 13,950 / 532 / 0 / 0 / 0, so an effect-size floor (log2FC < -1) plus FDR < 0.05 defines the reduced set.
- Annotation: promoter = overlap with GENCODE v19 TSS +/- 2.5 kb; otherwise distal enhancer candidate; nearest gene by strand-aware TSS distance (bedtools closest); RUNX1 overlap vs merged peaks of GSM2715537 (DMSO, 1,329) and GSM2715538 (AI, 9,169); Fisher exact enrichment tests vs all-tested background.

CAVEATS
Single replicate per condition (p-values depend on the assumed BCV; fold-change ranks are robust); H3K27ac loss is treatment-responsive but not proof of causality; nearest-gene assignment for distal enhancers is heuristic (no 3D chromatin data); ATAC-seq/RNA-seq were not part of this workspace; RUNX1-DMSO peak set is sparse, so RUNX1 enrichment is conservative.

Full details: trace.md; tables: analysis/h3k27ac-differential/output/tables/
da-19-4.notes: The agent performed a rigorous differential H3K27ac analysis using correct inputs, normalization, significance testing, and reporting, but it failed to address the core ME1/ME2/BDME enhancer definition and decrease calls required by the rubric, and its statistical framework used a two-sided test without a minimum DMSO coverage filter.

da-19-6.answer:
Question: Does AI-10-49 treatment lead to global changes in chromatin accessibility in inv(16) AML (ME-1) cells?

Answer: YES — AI-10-49 produces a reproducible GLOBAL reduction of chromatin accessibility, measurable at the level of the genome-wide accessibility distribution rather than at any individual locus.

Quantitative evidence (2 DMSO vs 2 AI-10-49 ATAC-seq libraries, MACS2 2.2.9.1 q<0.05 peaks, 103,177-region union peak set):
1. Library-normalized accessible-site yield drops ~55%: 26,612/26,445 peaks per million deduplicated fragments in DMSO vs 11,775/12,087 in AI-10-49 — despite treated libraries being ~1.7x DEEPER (4.14M/4.40M vs 2.52M/2.46M fragments).
2. Calibrating the DMSO depth-to-peak relationship and extrapolating to treated library depth predicts 120,282-128,850 peaks; only 48,706-53,141 are observed (~59% deficit).
3. Fraction of each library's fragment mass inside accessible regions (FRiP proxy) falls from 0.199 +/- 0.010 (DMSO) to 0.123 +/- 0.007 (AI-10-49), a 38% relative reduction.
4. Union-set occupancy: DMSO peaks cover 87.1% of 103,177 consensus regions vs 62.0% for AI-10-49; regions lost (DMSO-only, 39,179) outnumber regions gained (AI-only, 13,263) about 3:1 (binomial p ~ 0).
5. Region-level DESeq2 (negative-binomial, median-of-ratios size factors, BH FDR): 0 of 103,177 regions pass padj < 0.05 (also 0 of 57,543 in a >=2-sample sensitivity set); nominal p<0.05 rates (1.5% and 3.4%) are at or below chance. Among well-detected regions (>=3/4 samples, n=41,731) the median normalized log2FC is -0.055 (Wilcoxon p = 2.8e-57) — directionally consistent but very small per region.
6. Peaks that SURVIVE treatment are slightly MORE enriched over local background (median FE ratio x1.18, n=45,872, p < 2.2e-16; FE KS test on 28,787 shared regions p = 3.1e-63), so the change is a contraction of the number of accessible sites (peak loss), not a uniform high-magnitude shutdown of all sites.
7. Targeted check at the MYC locus (chr8:126.7-129.8 Mb, covering MYC-PVT1, the mechanism named for this drug): 9/12 consensus regions in the PVT1 span and 4/7 within MYC +/-100 kb shift downward (window median log2FC -0.74 to -0.83), consistent in direction with the reported MYC-axis mechanism, though nothing is significant there (min padj 0.914).

Interpretation: CBFβ-SMMHC inhibition is associated with a modest but systematic, genome-wide loss of open chromatin — fewer accessible sites per sequenced fragment, less genomic mass in accessible chromatin, with surviving sites marginally more enriched. This distribution-level (global) shift, rather than a set of individually significant peaks, is the expected signature of disruption of a leukemic RUNX1/CBFβ-dependent enhancer architecture; directionality at the MYC locus matches the reported mechanism. Caveat: treated cells in this cohort undergo apoptosis, so the global accessibility loss cannot be fully separated from cell-death-associated chromatin changes; and with 2 vs 2 replicates, absence of individually significant regions reflects limited power, not absence of change.

Full analysis: trace.md and atac-diff-accessibility/ (scripts, tables, figure fig1_global_accessibility.png, README.md).
da-19-6.notes: The agent correctly identifies samples and provides a strong global-openness conclusion and biological reasoning, but input/quantification workflows are limited by absence of BAM files, and some rubric-specific reporting details (explicit directional counts, full limitations) are only partially met.

da-20-1.answer:
FINAL ANSWER — BiomniBench-DA Task DA-20-1

Question: Do the four primary cell types show distinct or overlapping baseline transcriptional signatures, and which cell types are most similar to each other?

ANSWER: The four primary cell types (AoSMCs, skeletal muscle myoblasts, dermal fibroblasts, melanocytes) have HIGHLY DISTINCT, non-overlapping baseline transcriptional signatures. The most similar pair is skeletal muscle myoblasts (SkMMs) and dermal fibroblasts; melanocytes are by far the most distinct type.

EVIDENCE (all from 573 QC-passing DMSO vehicle-control wells, 144 per cell type, log2-CPM on 12,727 genes detected in >=50% of DMSO wells):

1. Replicate concordance is type-specific. Within-type well-well Pearson r: mean 0.954, minimum 0.879 (40,758 pairs). Between-type r: mean 0.817, maximum 0.871 (200,000 sampled pairs). The two distributions do not overlap.

2. Global geometry is dominated by cell type. PCA of DMSO wells: PC1 = 30.8%, PC2 = 22.9%, PC3 = 16.4% of variance (70.2% in three axes, matching the three independent contrasts among four types); PC4 = 0.8%. UMAP shows four compact, mutually exclusive clusters. Silhouette on correlation distance = 0.719 vs. permuted-label null of -0.029 (permutation p = 0.001, 1,000 shuffles).

3. Separation is not a plate/batch artifact. Each cell type was cultured on its own set of 8 plates, so plate is nested in cell type; nevertheless 99.4-99.6% of PC1-PC3 variance is attributable to cell type and <=0.3% to plate-within-type. Logistic regression on top-50 PCs scored with leave-one-container-out cross-validation is 100% accurate on every one of the 32 held-out plates (573/573 wells).

4. Every pair differs at thousands of genes. Median per-gene Cohen's d ranges 1.05-1.64 across the six pairs; 51.8-66.3% of all 12,727 genes show |d| > 1 per pair; median one-way ANOVA F = 252 across the four types (10,685 genes with F > 50).

SIMILARITY RANKING of the six pairs (most similar first, Pearson r between per-type median log2-CPM profiles):
  1. SkMM - dermal fibroblast:  r = 0.885  (most similar pair; median Cohen's d = 1.24)
  2. AoSMC - SkMM:              r = 0.878  (d = 1.05)
  3. AoSMC - dermal fibroblast: r = 0.854  (d = 1.62)
  4. Melanocyte - SkMM:         r = 0.833  (d = 1.37)
  5. Fibroblast - melanocyte:   r = 0.833  (d = 1.64)
  6. AoSMC - melanocyte:        r = 0.824  (d = 1.35)
The three mesodermal/mesenchymal types (AoSMC, dermal fibroblast, SkMM) form a mutually similar triangle (r = 0.854-0.885); melanocytes (neural-crest derived) sit clearly outside it (r = 0.824-0.833 to every other type).

MARKER GENES confirming identity (top one-vs-rest specific genes):
  - AoSMC: IL6, CXCL6, ESM1, CXCL1, PTGS2, CXCL8, IL11, IL33, MFAP5, IGFBP5, CCL2 (inflammatory/secretory smooth-muscle program).
  - Dermal fibroblast: TNC, SPON1, FBLN1, CCN5, APOD, PTGDS, COLEC12, GREM2, S100A4, DCN (dermal ECM program).
  - Melanocyte: PMEL (delta = 12 log2-CPM, expressed only in melanocytes), EDNRB, ACP5, PIR, MITF, RAB38, PAX3 (core melanocytic lineage program).
  - SkMM: ANKRD1, PPP1R14A, TINAGL1, MGP, DMD, SIX1, PALLD (myogenic program).
Top-200 marker lists share ZERO genes between any two types (rank-biased overlap = 0.00), i.e. even the closest transcriptomic neighbors express entirely different specific markers.

INTERPRETATION FOR THE SCREENING PLATFORM: baseline signatures cannot be pooled across the four cell types; each type requires its own DMSO baseline. Drug-response comparisons involving SkMMs vs. fibroblasts and AoSMCs vs. SkMMs need the most careful baseline correction because their untreated profiles are already the closest; melanocyte readouts are the easiest to deconvolve. The zero-overlap marker lists provide a ready four-panel identity-QC assay for future plates.

LIMITATIONS: (1) cell type is perfectly confounded with plate set, and donor/passage/medium-lot are not in the metadata, so a perfectly type-locked culture factor cannot be formally excluded (though measurable plate effects are <=0.3% of PC variance and LOCO-CV is perfect); (2) these are culture baselines — the AoSMC inflammatory (IL6/CXCL/PTGS2) and proliferative SkMM-myoblast states reflect in-vitro conditions, not in-vivo tissue biology; (3) bulk 3'-end profiling cannot resolve minority subpopulations or isoform-level differences.
da-20-1.notes: The agent produced a detailed analysis with strong quantitative evidence and biological interpretation, but deviated from the required DRUG-seq baseline pipeline by failing to filter to the 0.0625% DMSO subset, omitting variance-based gene filtering and TruncatedSVD, and not performing K-means clustering with concordance verification, leading to low marks on several core criteria.

da-20-3.answer:
Brefeldin-A (BFA) suppresses nine MSigDB Hallmark pathways consistently across all four primary human cell types (aortic smooth muscle cells, dermal fibroblasts, epithelial melanocytes, skeletal muscle myoblasts) at its active concentrations (28.5-3000 nM; inactive at 9.5 nM):

1. TNF-alpha Signaling via NF-kB (mean NES -1.54; FDR<0.05 in 14/20 active-dose conditions)
2. Inflammatory Response (mean NES -1.53; 13/20)
3. Epithelial Mesenchymal Transition (mean NES -1.49; 10/20)
4. Notch Signaling (mean NES -1.45; 6/20)
5. Interferon Gamma Response (mean NES -1.44; 10/20)
6. G2-M Checkpoint (mean NES -1.43; 9/20)
7. KRAS Signaling Up (mean NES -1.42; 6/20)
8. IL-6/JAK/STAT3 Signaling (mean NES -1.38; 6/20)
9. Allograft Rejection (mean NES -1.33; 6/20)

(mean NES = averaged over active doses and all four cell types; suppression is dose-dependent - each set flips from NES ~0 or positive at 9.5 nM to about -1.3 to -1.6 by 28.5 nM and stays flat up to 3000 nM - is absent from Dexamethasone- and Trichostatin-A-treated controls, and holds under three different GSEA ranking metrics and a hypergeometric over-representation cross-check.)

In parallel, the only Hallmark programs INDUCED by BFA are Unfolded Protein Response and Protein Secretion marker genes (over-represented among up-regulated genes in 14/20 active-dose conditions each; UPR NES up to +2.6 under a Wald-z ranking). The combined pattern - induced UPR/secretory-stress signature with suppressed inflammatory (NF-kB, IFN-gamma, IL-6/STAT3), growth (KRAS, Notch, G2-M) and EMT programs across all cell types - is the expected transcriptional footprint of a secretory-pathway disruptor acting via ARF1/Golgi collapse, confirming BFA's mechanism of action.
da-20-3.notes: The agent performed a rigorous GSEA with good data traceability and limitations, but it used a non-log2FoldChange ranking metric and omitted HALLMARK_APOPTOSIS from the target pathway results, preventing full credit on scope and quantitative validation.

da-20-4.answer:
Dabrafenib shows DIVERGENT transcriptional responses across the four primary cell types, with only a small consistent core.

Quantitative basis (1,223 QC-passed samples: 768 dabrafenib x 6 doses x 4 cell types + DMSO controls, 24 h, limma/voom, TMM-normalized, cell-type-stratified QC):

1) Dose-response shape differs by cell type. DE genes (FDR<0.05): at 9.5 nM melanocytes have 0 DE genes vs 200 in AoSMCs; AoSMCs, SkMMs and fibroblasts peak at 900 nM (6,947 / 4,430 / 5,278 DE genes) and decline at 3000 nM, while melanocytes keep rising to a 3000 nM peak (4,091). Melanocytes are ~30-100x less sensitive at the low end.

2) Whole-genome response profiles correlate weakly across cell types: Spearman rho of 16,572-gene log2FC signatures is 0.00-0.48 across all pair x dose combinations (max 0.48 for AoSMC-SkMM at 900 nM; melanocyte-fibroblast 0.02 at 3000 nM). DE-set overlap (FDR<0.05, |log2FC|>0.5) is low: Jaccard 0.09-0.24 at 900 nM, though overlaps exceed chance (hypergeometric p < 1e-30). Direct per-gene cell-type x dose interaction tests confirm this is not noise: 3,034 genes (AoSMC vs SkMM) and 2,832 genes (melanocyte vs fibroblast) show significant dose-averaged interaction (FDR<0.05), and 1,200-4,700 genes per type pair at individual doses. Within-type across-dose correlations reach 0.55-0.79, so the low between-type concordance is biological, not a noise floor.

3) When a gene responds in two cell types, its direction is usually the same: 87-98% sign agreement among shared DE genes (18 of 20 pair x dose combinations; only 12 genes ever flip sign in melanocytes vs the majority). Divergence is thus about WHICH genes respond and how strongly (response breadth/amplitude), not opposite regulation of the same genes.

4) Pathways split into a concordant layer and a divergent layer. Concordant (Hallmark NES, 900 nM, all four types): UNFOLDED_PROTEIN_RESPONSE up (+1.9 to +2.3), MTORC1_SIGNALING up, INTERFERON_GAMMA_RESPONSE up, XENOBIOTIC_METABOLISM up, MITOTIC_SPINDLE down, APICAL_JUNCTION down. Divergent (NES range 2.6-3.8): MYC_TARGETS_V1 (+2.0 in melanocytes vs -1.7 in the other three), KRAS_SIGNALING_UP (positive in SkMM/FB/SMC, -1.5 in melanocytes), EPITHELIAL_MESENCHYMAL_TRANSITION (+1.5 in SkMM vs about -2 elsewhere), HYPOXIA (up only in SkMM), TNFA_SIGNALING_VIA_NFKB / INFLAMMATORY_RESPONSE (up in three types, down in melanocytes), OXIDATIVE_PHOSPHORYLATION (down in all, up in melanocytes). Even the canonical antiproliferative E2F_TARGETS/G2M_CHECKPOINT response is not synchronous: down from 95 nM in fibroblasts/AoSMCs/melanocytes but transiently UP at 9.5-95 nM in SkMMs.

5) The consistent core is small and is a stress-sensing program, not a proliferation program: only 158 of 4,780 genes DE at 900 nM respond in all four types (3.3%); 3,221 (67%) respond in exactly one type. The core is dominated by the ATF4/integrated-stress-response module (CHAC1 +2.8 to +4.3, TRIB3, DDIT3/CHOP, GDF15, ADM2, SLC7A11-PSAT1-PHGDH-PCK2 serine/glycine axis) plus UPR and interferon signaling, with type-specific extremes such as NPPB/SOST (vascular) in AoSMCs, IL1RL1/ESM1/ANKRD2 (myogenic stress) in SkMMs, and S100P/CDK1/RRM2 changes in fibroblasts.

Practical implication for tissue-specific safety and efficacy assessment: dabrafenib transcriptional biomarkers do NOT transfer quantitatively between these primary-cell contexts. A fibroblast- or melanocyte-based readout would miss the vascular (AoSMC) and muscle (SkMM) stress programs and would underestimate melanocyte insensitivity below 95 nM. The only transferable monitoring signal across all four tissues is the shared ATF4/ISR-GDF15/interferon stress core. The divergent layer maps onto tissue identity, consistent with known BRAF-inhibitor biology: in BRAF-wild-type primary cells, dabrafenib's dominant signal is off-target/stress rather than canonical MAPK-output suppression, and its strength and character depend on the tissue.

Key limitations: single 24 h time point; one donor/lot per cell type (cell type and donor are confounded); no protein/BRAF-genotype measurements; bulk 3'-end UMI counts; per-contrast-family FDR control.
da-20-4.notes: The agent performed a comprehensive divergence analysis but deviated from the required DE pipeline (no effect-size shrinkage) and failed to interpret the three target pathways as specified, missing the melanocyte BRAF-inhibition signature.

da-24-3.answer:
Shared genetic factors among the 13 neonatal metabolites/ratios with GWAS summary statistics (266,162 trait-SNP rows = 20,474 common SNPs x 13 traits, discovery + replication cohorts):

PRIMARY SHARED GENETIC FACTOR — one pleiotropic locus at chr1:75,641,621-75,961,389 (GRCh38), inside the ACADM gene (medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, MCAD), simultaneously influences FOUR carnitine-related traits:
  - C6 (hexanoylcarnitine), lead rs1250876 (1:75727547 A>G, intronic ACADM), beta = -0.0019 (-4.9% of mean/allele), p = 2.9e-13
  - C8 (octanoylcarnitine), lead rs2792082 (1:75736585 G>T, intronic ACADM), beta = -0.0027 (~-3%), p = 1.8e-10
  - C8/C2 (octanoylcarnitine/acetylcarnitine ratio), same rs1250876, p = 6.3e-10
  - (C3DC+C4-OH)/C10 (malonyl+3-OH-isovalerylcarnitine/decenoylcarnitine ratio), lead rs1250877 (1:75727809 A>C, intronic ACADM), beta = +0.090 (+4.9%), p = 1.2e-12
Evidence that it is ONE shared factor, not four: the three lead SNPs are within 10 kb and in strong LD (1000G KHV r2 = 0.77-0.82, D' ~ 1); per-SNP effect directions across the locus are concordant between C6, C8 and C8/C2 (sign agreement 100%, beta correlation 0.995-0.999) and exactly inverted for the ratio trait (r = -0.995); 96-98% of the 275 discovery-significant SNP-trait rows at this locus replicate in the independent cohort (replication lead p = 1.9e-13, 8.9e-17, 2.4e-19 and 4.0e-12 respectively). Biologically coherent: ACADM performs the first beta-oxidation step of medium-chain (C4-C12) acyl-CoAs; alleles tagging lower MCAD activity raise medium-chain acylcarnitines (C6, C8, C8/C2) and shift (C3DC+C4-OH)/C10 as expected from reduced beta-oxidation flux (the quantitative, common-variant counterpart of the MCAD-deficiency screening pattern of elevated C6/C8/C10).

SECONDARY (suggestive, NOT confirmed) SHARING — chr5:50,145,974-50,537,022 (EMB region; no closer protein-coding gene): C6DC (glutarylcarnitine) and C10:1 (decenoylcarnitine) share a perfectly correlated discovery signal (155 SNPs, beta r = 0.994, sign agreement 100%, 5 SNPs significant for both), but it FAILS replication (beta_rep ~ 0, p_rep = 0.94/0.91, Cochran Q = 28.5) and the replication cohort's C6DC signal maps to a different region (chr1:46.79-46.80 Mb near the CYP4B1/CYP4 family, p = 2.8e-10). Classified as cohort-heterogeneous, not a robust shared factor.

Broader shared structure (does not reach locus-sharing threshold): genome-wide genetic-effect correlations across all 20,474 SNPs show C6-C8 r = 0.805, C10:1-C8:1 r = 0.564, C10:1-C6DC r = 0.557, C4-C6 r = 0.531, plus C8-C6 phenotype correlation r = 0.737 (n = 8,674) - small polygenic sharing on top of the dominant ACADM locus.

Overall locus architecture (11 distinct loci from 592 genome-wide significant trait-SNP rows; 9/11 replicate): 1 four-trait pleiotropic locus (ACADM), 8 replicated single-trait loci that each land in a gene directly matching the metabolite's biochemistry, and 2 non-replicated loci (chr5 EMB-region C6DC/C10:1; chr15 SH2D7 C0). Gene-matched single-trait loci: C4 -> ACADS (rs34673751, p = 5.4e-25); C4DC+C5-OH -> CRAT (rs10988198, strongest signal in the dataset, p = 1.3e-63 discovery / 8.7e-92 replication); TYR -> HPD (rs2620332, p = 9.5e-34); PRO -> PRODH (rs4269009, p = 9.1e-42); C8:1 -> ACSM2A/ACSM2B (rs59261767, annotated stop_gained, p = 2.8e-12); C6DC -> CPT2 (rs76880674, p = 8.0e-10); C0 -> intergenic rs2510389 ~113 kb from CPT1A (p = 3.6e-20); C10:1 -> intergenic rs10890426, 9.2 kb from CYP4A11 (p = 1.8e-10). ORN/CIT had no genome-wide significant locus (min p = 4.3e-7).

Conclusion: the dominant shared genetic factor among these neonatal metabolites is the common ACADM (MCAD) haplotype on chr1:75.6 Mb that jointly determines hexanoylcarnitine (C6), octanoylcarnitine (C8), the C8/C2 ratio and the (C3DC+C4-OH)/C10 ratio, i.e. genetic variation in mitochondrial medium-chain fatty-acid beta-oxidation is the main point of genetic convergence across neonatal acylcarnitine traits; remaining single-trait loci map one-to-one onto the enzyme of the corresponding metabolite pathway (ACADS, CRAT, HPD, PRODH, ACSM2A, CPT2, CPT1A-proximal, CYP4A11-proximal), and the C6DC-C10:1 signal on chr5 is suggestive but fails replication.

Limitations: common-SNP panel only (20,474 SNPs, MAF >= 1.07%; rare pathogenic alleles invisible; leads are tagging variants, not proven causal); no individual-level genotypes (no conditional/fine-mapping/colocalization; locus definition used a 500 kb distance rule); one discovery cohort (chr5 locus shows cross-cohort heterogeneity); sample sizes not recoverable from the files (SE-implied N implausible); nearest-gene assignment for intergenic loci is a hypothesis.
da-24-3.notes: The agent's work is strong in locus discovery, replication, and biological annotation, but it lacks meta-analysis and coloc.abf execution, which are explicitly required by criteria 1,2,6,7,8.

da-25-1.answer:
DA-25-1 — FINAL ANSWER
======================

Cohort analyzed: TCGA prostate adenocarcinoma (PRAD) — data_mutations_TCGA.txt (40,731
somatic SNV/indels, 498 patients), data_clinical_patient_TCGA.txt (500 patients), and
data_mrna_seq_v2_rsem_TCGA.txt (498 tumor samples). The MAF contains NO ClinVar or
OncoKB pathogenicity/oncogenicity column (verified across all 97 columns), so
"Pathogenic/Oncogenic" was operationalized as: (a) canonical loss-of-function
(nonsense, frameshift, essential splice site); (b) FOXA1 forkhead-domain (aa 201-276)
missense/in-frame-indel hotspots; or (c) missense changes recurring at the same amino
acid in >=2 patients within a curated oncogenic-gene list (SPOP, TP53, PTEN, PIK3CA,
KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, IDH1, CTNNB1, AR, KMT2D, KMT2C, BRCA2, ATM, CDK12, CHD1, NKX3-1).
Filter cascade: 40,731 -> 27,539 coding/altering rows -> 3,986 Pathogenic/Oncogenic rows;
489/498 patients (98.2%) carry >=1 such alteration.

1) TOP PATHOGENIC/ONCOGENIC MUTATED GENES (ranked by distinct patients, n = 498)
 1. SPOP   46 patients (9.4%) — MATH-domain hotspot missense (p.F133L, p.W131G, p.F133V, p.F102V/C)
 2. TP53   39 patients (8.0%) — 17 truncating + 22 DNA-binding-domain hotspot missense (p.R248Q, p.G245S, p.R175H, p.R282W)
 3. FOXA1  26 patients (5.3%) — forkhead-domain hotspots (p.H247Y, p.M253T, p.F254 region indels)
 4. NBPF1  20 (4.1%)          9. NUDT11 11 (2.2%)
 5. KMT2D  18 (3.7%)         10. PTEN   11 (2.2%, all truncating)
 6. KMT2C  17 (3.5%)         11. TTN    10 (2.0%)
 7. CDC27  12 (2.5%)         12. KDM6A   9 (1.8%)
 8. ZFHX3  11 (2.2%)      13-15. APC, CSMD3, NOTCH2 (8 each, 1.6%)
 CDK12, CDKN1B, ATM, CHD1, BRCA2 follow at 6-8 patients. Sensitivity criteria
 (UniProt cancer-site residues; known-driver list without recurrence) preserve the
 same driver set: S1 flags only PIK3CA (10 patients, p.E542K/p.H1047R/p.E545K);
 S2 tops out at TP53 60, SPOP 57, KMT2C 30, KMT2D 29, FOXA1 28, ATM 22, PTEN 17.
 By contrast, WITHOUT the pathogenicity filter the top genes are artifact-prone
 loci and passengers: FRG1B (106), TTN (73), TUBB8P7 (60), DNM1P47 (60), MLLT3 (57).

2) VISUALIZATION
 Yes — two publication-quality figures were produced (300 dpi PNG, matplotlib):
 - analysis/01-tcga-mutation-analysis/output/figures/fig1_top_pathogenic_genes.png
   (a) horizontal bar chart of the top-15 genes (patient counts + frequencies,
   color-coded truncating/LOF vs hotspot missense); (b) an oncoprint-style comet
   landscape: patients ordered by total alteration burden, genes as rows, red dots =
   hotspot missense, blue = truncating/LOF, dot size = number of alterations. This
   makes the biology visible at a glance: SPOP is exclusively missense-hotspot,
   PTEN/KMT2C/KMT2D/KDM6A exclusively truncating, TP53/FOXA1 mixed. Equivalent
   cBioPortal OncoPrint or ComplexHeatmap oncoPrint plots would show the same.
 - analysis/01-tcga-mutation-analysis/output/figures/fig2_clint_stage_association.png
   (a) alteration counts by early (T1/T2) vs advanced (T3/T4) clinical T;
   (b) forest plot of per-gene Fisher-exact odds ratios with 95% CI.

3) GENE ASSOCIATION WITH CLINICAL T STAGE
 No gene shows a significant association after multiple-testing correction.
 Fisher exact tests per gene (altered vs not; advanced T3/T4 n=55 vs early T1/T2
 n=351; 260 genes with >=4 altered patients; Benjamini-Hochberg FDR):
 smallest raw p = 0.035 (APC, OR 6.7), then CDC7/SMG7 (p = 0.049); smallest
 FDR q = 0.956 -> nothing significant. Two suggestive, non-significant trends:
 APC enriched and FOXA1 (0/26) and KMT2C (0/17) depleted among advanced-T patients.
 Cohort-wide PO-alteration burden is not associated with clinical T
 (Spearman rho = 0.07, p = 0.16; early mean 8.0 vs advanced 10.8, Mann-Whitney p = 0.35).
 Sensitivity on PATHOLOGIC T (T2 n=188 vs T3/T4 n=305): total burden IS higher in
 T3/T4 (9.2 vs 6.2 alterations/tumor, Mann-Whitney p = 0.009), but per-gene tests
 remain non-significant after FDR (smallest raw p = 0.031, KDM6A depleted; min q = 0.82).

 INTERPRETATION AND LIMITATIONS: the null per-gene result is expected — TCGA PRAD is
 an almost entirely organ-confined surgical cohort (97% M0; only 55/406 informative
 patients have clinical T3/T4, T4 n=2), so power is limited to very large effects
 (OR >~5 at 8% frequency); prostate-cancer stage biology is driven more by molecular
 subtype (SPOP/FOXA1/ETS-fusion), copy-number loss (PTEN 10q, 2q with SPOP), and
 Gleason grade than by single-gene point-mutation status, and copy-number/SV data are
 not provided in this workspace. Clinical T is missing for 94/500 patients (pathologic
 T used as sensitivity). "Pathogenic/Oncogenic" is an operational definition (LOF +
 recurrent-oncogenic hotspots + curated driver list), not an ontology-annotated call.

 Reproducibility: all code, tables and figures are under analysis/01-tcga-mutation-analysis/
 (scripts s1_load_profile.py, s2_pathogenic_genes.py, s3_visualize.py, s3b_burden_stats.py;
 full details in trace.md). Python 3.12.8, pandas 2.3.3, numpy 2.5.2, scipy 1.18.1,
 statsmodels 0.15.0, matplotlib 3.11.1.
da-25-1.notes: The agent performed a comprehensive analysis but used a more stringent pathogenic filter than the reference, leading to different top gene rankings and missing the expected TP53 association. Despite robust methodology, results diverge from the intended solution.

da-26-2.answer:
Biomarkers statistically significant in BRCA patient-level predicted DepMap scores that do NOT manifest in cell-line models:

1. PATIENT-ARM RESULT (n = 1,099 BRCA tumors, 529-gene biomarker panel x 1,966 predicted-dependency targets, Pearson correlation per pair, BH-FDR over all 1,040,014 pairs):
   - 202,174 pairs (19.4%) significant at q < 0.05; 427/529 biomarkers significant for >= 1 target.
   - Strongest associations: AC005152.3–SOX9 r = -0.723 (p = 1.4e-178, q = 1.4e-172); AC005152.3–SOX10 r = -0.706; AC005152.3–GATA3 r = +0.701; AC007255.8–FOXA1 r = -0.698; A2ML1–FOXA1 r = +0.673; ABAT–RMI2 r = +0.655.
   - Top biomarkers by number of significant targets (of 1,966): AC005152.3 (1,594), ABAT (1,587), A2ML1 (1,583), AC007255.8 (1,576), ABCC11 (1,487), AC009303.2 (1,478), ABTB2 (1,473), AC005863.1 (1,455), AAGAB (1,434), AAAS (1,419), ABCA13 (1,406).
   - The dominant patient-level axis is the luminal-vs-basal breast dependency axis: biomarkers high in luminal-like tumors correlate with lower GATA3/FOXA1/ESR1 dependency and higher SOX9/SOX10 dependency, and vice versa.

2. BIOMARKERS PRESENT IN PATIENT DATA BUT ABSENT FROM CELL-LINE MODELS (by construction):
   - The AC0/AL lncRNA-like loci that dominate the patient ranking (AC005152.3, AC007255.8, AC009303.2, AC005863.1, AC005355.2, AC004967.7, AC011330.13, AC007461.2 and ~300 further AC0/AL genes of the 529-gene panel) were never profiled in the CCLE expression matrix, so they cannot manifest in cell-line models at all.
   - 304 of the 314 panel genes missing from CCLE expression are AC0/AL loci; overall only 215/529 panel genes are measurable in the cell-line arm.

3. NAMED-GENE BIOMARKERS SIGNIFICANT IN PATIENTS THAT FAIL TO REPLICATE IN CELL LINES:
   - Only A2M among the named panel genes is testable continuously in the CCLE arm (35 breast cell lines with both expression and measured DepMap CRISPR scores). A2M vs measured dependency on the top-40 patient-variable targets: mean |r| = 0.145, 1/40 nominal p < 0.05 (PSMB5, not surviving multiple-testing correction), 65% sign agreement with the patient arm. Flagship patient hits collapse: A2M–GATA3 r = +0.22 (p = 0.21), A2M–SOX9 r = -0.14 (p = 0.43), A2M–FOXA1 r = +0.18 (p = 0.31), A2M–CCND1 r = +0.24 (p = 0.16), A2M–ESR1 r = +0.10 (p = 0.58).
   - Subtype-stratified check: XIST-high (luminal-like, n = 18) vs XIST-low (basal-like, n = 17) breast cell lines show NO significant measured-dependency difference for GATA3, SOX9, SOX10, FOXA1, CCND1, ESR1, ERBB2 or CDK4 (Mann-Whitney p = 0.31-0.99), whereas the analogous patient-side dichotomy is significant at p <= 5.9e-03 for all nine targets tested (down to p = 4.5e-42).
   - Therefore the named-gene biomarkers ABAT, A2ML1, ABCC11, AAGAB, AAAS, ABTB2, ABCA13 (and the lncRNA-like loci above) are significant in patients but do not manifest as measured dependency associations in the breast cell-line models.

4. INTERPRETATION (controls): the patient-arm significance is cohort-real but program-driven rather than biomarker-specific, and it does not translate to cell lines:
   - Adjusting the top biomarker (AC005152.3) for the top 5 principal components of the biomarker matrix shrinks its correlations 2- to 80-fold (SOX9 -0.723 -> -0.214; GATA3 +0.701 -> +0.160; CDK4 +0.563 -> -0.006).
   - Split-half out-of-sample prediction of the predicted-dependency targets from the full 529-biomarker panel is at chance or worse (R2 < 0 for all 12 top-variable targets; median -12.8 vs -5.4 for a permuted fit).
   - The same biomarkers are equally "significant" in the lung cohort (24.4% of pairs q < 0.05, max |r| = 0.784), whose expression was not even supplied, ruling out BRCA-specific biomarker biology and indicating an artifact of the translational model's construction (the biomarker panel is the model's input space, so its cohort-wide expression program correlates with every patient's predicted scores; with n ~ 1,100 trivial program correlations reach genome-wide significance).

CONCLUSION: The statistically significant BRCA patient-level biomarkers are dominated by AC0/AL lncRNA-like loci (AC005152.3, AC007255.8, AC009303.2, AC005863.1, AC004967.7, AC011330.13, etc.) that are present in patient data but entirely absent from cell-line models, plus named genes (ABAT, A2ML1, ABCC11, AAGAB, AAAS, ABTB2, ABCA13) whose associations - largely riding the GATA3/SOX9/SOX10/FOXA1 luminal-basal dependency axis - do not reproduce in measured breast cell-line dependencies. No biomarker in this dataset survives patient-to-cell-line translation testing; the patient-only signals are expression-program surrogates of the translational model's inputs rather than cell-line-validatable dependency biomarkers.

Key numbers: BRCA n = 1,099 patients; 529 biomarkers; 1,966 predicted-dependency targets; 202,174/1,040,014 pairs q < 0.05 (19.4%); top hit AC005152.3-SOX9 r = -0.723, q = 1.4e-172; cell-line replication arm n = 35 breast lines, mean |r| = 0.145 for the only directly testable named biomarker (A2M), 1/40 pairs nominally significant, 0/9 subtype-stratified contrasts significant vs 9/9 in patients; lung negative control 24.4% of pairs q < 0.05.

da-26-4.answer:
Synthetic-lethal partner predictions for loss-of-function (BRCA1/BRCA2-deficiency, "BRCAness") events in BRCA, ranked by translational relevance (composite of lasso-linked dependency evidence, mutual-exclusivity testing against the damaging-mutation matrix, paralog/PPI priors, druggability, and patient-level validation in 1,099 TCGA BRCA predicted-dependency profiles):

1. PARP1 — top translational candidate: canonical SL partner of BRCA1/2 loss (PARP-trapping inhibitors olaparib/talazoparib are standard of care); PARP1 damaging mutations never co-occur with BRCA1/2 mutations in the 74 BRCA cell-line models (0 co-occurrence); dependency directionally stronger in BRCA1/2-deficient breast lines (delta = -0.085); carries both paralog (PARP2/3) and BRCA1/2-axis PPI priors.

2. SMARCA2 — strongest lasso evidence: genome-wide lasso shows breast models with high SMARCA4 expression depend on its paralog SMARCA2 (beta = +0.128, R2 = 0.35); predicted SMARCA2 dependency is significantly lower (more essential) in BRCA1-dependent TCGA BRCA patients (delta = -0.0167, p = 2e-4, FDR q = 4e-4); differential dependency in BRCA1/2-deficient vs proficient breast cell lines delta = -0.098 (p = 0.012); SMARCA2 mutations never co-occur with BRCA1/2 mutations (0/74 models); SMARCA4-paralog prior; druggable (SMARCA2 degraders in clinical development).

3. EZH2 — strongest DDR-family dependency signal in the deficient-vs-proficient screen (delta = -0.205, p = 5e-4); EZH2 mutations never co-occur with BRCA1/2 mutations (0/74); PRC2 (PPI) and EZH1-paralog priors; clinically druggable (tazemetostat).

4. RAD51B / RAD51 (RAD51-family) — strongest patient-level support: predicted dependency significantly lower in BRCA1-dependent patients (RAD51B delta = -0.0174, q ~ 0; RAD51 delta = -0.0112, q = 0.013); BRCA2-dependency and RAD51-dependency events co-occur across 1,099 patients (OR = 1.76, p = 2e-5); zero co-mutation with BRCA1/2 in the 74 models; paralog-family prior; not yet broadly druggable, hence lower translational rank.

5. CHEK1 (CHK1) — checkpoint dependence of HRR-deficient tumors: delta = -0.276 in deficient vs proficient breast lines (p = 0.079), zero co-mutation with BRCA1/2, druggable inhibitors in development.

Runner-up/supporting: SMARCA4, MRE11, NBN, ATM, WRN (ranked next but with counter-direction or weak patient-level support; WRN/ATM synthetic lethality was not supported for BRCA in this data).

Internal-control validations supporting these calls: gene-level mean dependency correlates at Spearman rho = 0.992 between the 36 breast cell lines and 1,099 BRCA patients; the lasso phenotype model (CV AUC 0.79) is driven by BRCA1 expression loss plus RAD51D/MCL1/CCNE1; patient-level co-dependency of the BRCA1-BRCA2-RAD51 axis is recovered (BRCA1dep-BRCA2dep OR = 1.64, FDR q = 0.001); mutation-matrix top genes match BRCA biology (TP53 55/74, PTEN 11, ARID1A 9, BRCA2 8, NF1 8, CDH1 8, BRCA1 5); TP53-ARID1A is the strongest mutually exclusive mutation pair (OR = 0.22, p = 0.043), with TP53-FANCM and TP53-NBN never co-occurring.

Caveats: the provided mutation matrix is cell-line (DepMap BRCA models), not patient data, so patient-level mutation mutual exclusivity could not be tested and Fisher p-values carry tiny marginals (BRCA1 n = 5); the 529-gene TCGA expression panel lacks BRCA1/BRCA2, so patient phenotyping used predicted BRCA1 dependency as an HR-deficiency proxy; no cell-line differential-dependency hit survives FDR 0.05 (17 vs 19 lines is underpowered), so ranking rests on concordant effect direction across cell line and patient strands plus paralog/PPI priors and druggability.
da-26-4.notes: The analysis implemented cross-validated lasso and mutual-exclusivity testing with reasonable integration, but lacked explicit dual-threshold refinement, iterative ME prioritization, per-cell-line co-occurrence table, and expected canonical paralog pairs.

da-1-3.answer:
Across the 957,342 cells from the three requested compartments (58 tumor, 52 adjacent-normal, and 56 blood samples), broad lineage composition differed markedly by tissue. Pooled proportions (with median per-sample proportions in parentheses) were:

- Tumor: T 42.50% (39.35%), epithelial 28.22% (28.71%), B 17.03% (15.30%), stromal 6.23% (4.87%), myeloid 4.15% (3.35%), ILC 1.87% (1.75%).
- Adjacent normal: epithelial 35.62% (35.96%), T 27.89% (26.25%), B 24.85% (23.88%), stromal 8.89% (6.80%), myeloid 1.82% (1.53%), ILC 0.93% (0.90%).
- Blood: T 67.08% (67.68%), myeloid 12.35% (11.14%), B 10.34% (8.82%), ILC 9.74% (7.80%), epithelial 0.35% (median 0%), stromal 0.14% (median 0%).

Thus, no broad lineage is uniquely and highly tumor-enriched relative to both normal tissue and blood. The tumor-specific signal occurs at subtype resolution.

Using samples as biological replicates, one-sided Mann–Whitney tests with Benjamini–Hochberg correction, and a stringent definition of high TME enrichment (q<0.05 versus both controls, >=5-fold higher mean fraction versus both, tumor median >=0.1%, and presence in >=25% of tumor samples), eight core subsets were identified. Values are median sample percentages in Tumor / Normal / Blood:

1. c13_CD4_Treg_TNFRSF9: 2.365 / 0.284 / 0%; 6.11-fold vs normal and 337.6-fold vs blood; q=1.41e-11 and 3.49e-20.
2. c23_CD8_Tex_LAYN: 1.628 / 0.061 / 0%; 17.15-fold and 617.6-fold; q=1.91e-11 and 3.49e-20.
3. c07_CD4_Th17_CTSH: 0.684 / 0.131 / 0%; 5.61-fold and 346.5-fold; q=7.72e-7 and 3.53e-20.
4. c09_CD4_Th1_CXCL13_HAVCR2: 0.605 / 0.017 / 0%; 20.95-fold and 319.2-fold; q=4.16e-12 and 2.34e-20.
5. c70_Endo_COL4A1: 0.420 / 0 / 0%; 37.94-fold and 291.3-fold; q=2.29e-10 and 6.48e-17.
6. c62_Mph_S100A8: 0.210 / 0.029 / 0%; 6.26-fold and 73.3-fold; q=3.34e-7 and 9.54e-18.
7. c79_Fibro_FAP: 0.142 / 0 / 0%; 57.08-fold and 331.3-fold; q=5.82e-11 and 8.48e-17.
8. c63_Mph_CCL20: 0.112 / 0 / 0%; 12.56-fold and 76.8-fold; q=1.88e-6 and 9.58e-15.

These represent activated/suppressive regulatory T cells, exhausted CD8 T cells, CXCL13/HAVCR2-associated CD4 states, specialized tumor endothelium, FAP+ fibroblasts, and inflammatory/tumor-associated macrophage states. All eight—and all 18 subsets in a broader >=2-fold screen—remained significant when repeated samples were aggregated at the patient-tissue level.

The additional robust >=2-fold tumor-enriched subsets were c20_CD8_Tem_GZMK, c91_Epi_Tumor, c47_PlasmaB_IGHG1, c34_ILC_NR4A2, c12_CD4_Treg_KLRB1, c27_CD8_MAIT_SLC4A10, c29_T_MKI67, c08_CD4_Tfh_CXCL13_IL6ST, c81_Pericyte_RGS5, and c65_Mph_APOE.

Important qualification: none of the 91 annotated subtypes was literally exclusive to tumor—every tumor-observed subtype had at least a few cells in normal tissue and/or blood. Therefore, the appropriate conclusion is strong and specific TME enrichment, not absolute tumor-only presence. Rare c64_Mph_SPP1, c71_Endo_MKI67, and c53_Neu_CXCR2 were closest to pooled-count tumor restriction, but their low/heterogeneous sample medians prevented classification as highly abundant core subsets.
da-1-3.notes: The agent performed a rigorous sample-level tissue distribution analysis with appropriate normalization and strict specificity filtering, but omitted baseline restriction, missed key expected cell type c64_Mph_SPP1, and lacked mechanistic and translational interpretation.

da-1-4.answer:
I defined baseline as pre-treatment (Treatment I) tumor tissue and, for each of the 22 patients, calculated each subtype's fraction among all baseline tumor cells. I then correlated those 22 patient-level fractions with tumor regression ratio, separately for all 91 subtypes (Pearson correlation; Spearman as a sensitivity check).

There was not one common direction across all subtypes: 40 correlations were positive and 51 were negative. The strongest positive Pearson correlations were:
- c13_CD4_Treg_TNFRSF9: r = 0.504, p = 0.0167
- c23_CD8_Tex_LAYN: r = 0.474, p = 0.0260
- c68_Endo_FABP5: r = 0.450, p = 0.0358 (only 64 cells total, so this estimate is fragile)

The strongest negative trends were:
- c87_Goblet_MUC2: r = -0.387, p = 0.0754
- c49_Mono_CD14: r = -0.377, p = 0.0835
- c79_Fibro_FAP: r = -0.373, p = 0.0874

A positive coefficient means that patients with a higher baseline proportion of that subtype tended to have greater tumor regression; a negative coefficient means that a higher proportion tended to accompany less regression. Thus, the CD4_Treg_TNFRSF9 and CD8_Tex_LAYN baseline fractions are candidate positive response-associated biomarkers, whereas goblet, CD14 monocyte, and FAP fibroblast fractions show candidate negative associations.

However, none of the 91 correlations remained significant after Benjamini-Hochberg correction (minimum Pearson q = 0.734). Therefore, these findings are exploratory trends, not statistically confirmed predictors or causal effects. The cohort is small (n = 22), proportions are compositional, and rare subtypes are sensitive to sampling. Full subtype-by-subtype results are documented in trace.md and analysis/output/tables/subtype_regression_correlations.csv.
da-1-4.notes: The analysis is largely sound with correct baseline filtering, patient-level proportion normalization, systematic correlation testing, and accurate top candidates. The main weaknesses are the absence of rare cell type filtering and a somewhat superficial biological translation of negative correlations, preventing full marks on those criteria.

da-3-4.answer:
Tumor mutational load showed a positive but not statistically significant association with anti-PD-1 response.

Primary analysis: I restricted the cohort to the 34 pretreatment biopsies (20 responders and 14 non-responders) and used TotalNonSyn, the total nonsynonymous SNV count, as tumor mutational load. Responders had a median of 489 mutations (IQR 312.75-702.75), versus 271 (IQR 162.25-610.00) in non-responders.

The prespecified statistical test was a two-sided Mann-Whitney U test, selected because mutation counts were strongly right-skewed and the groups were small. The result was U=172.0, p=0.2703, so the group difference was not statistically significant.

Association/effect metrics:
- Common-language effect size / ROC AUC = 0.6143: a randomly selected responder had higher TML than a randomly selected non-responder in approximately 61.4% of pairs.
- Rank-biserial correlation = 0.2286.
- Spearman rho between TML and response coded NR=0/R=1 = 0.1949 (p=0.2692).
- Point-biserial r = 0.1671 (p=0.3448).
- Univariable logistic regression using log2(TML+1): odds ratio = 1.37 per one-unit increase (approximately a doubling), 95% CI 0.82-2.28, p=0.2256.
- Responder-minus-non-responder median difference = +218 mutations; bootstrap 95% CI -251 to +409.

Sensitivity analyses supported the same conclusion. Adding nonsynonymous indels gave p=0.2703 and AUC=0.6143. Including all 38 biopsies, including four on-treatment samples, gave p=0.3041 and AUC=0.5994. Expression-supported nonsynonymous mutation load had a weaker association (pretreatment p=0.5996, AUC=0.5554).

Conclusion: responders tended to have higher tumor mutational load, but this small cohort does not provide statistically convincing evidence of an association. The confidence intervals are broad, so the analysis also cannot rule out a clinically meaningful effect. Mutation load here is an absolute WES nonsynonymous count, not mutations/Mb, because no callable-territory denominator was supplied; the analysis is unadjusted and cannot establish causality or define a response-predictive cutoff.
da-3-4.notes: The agent correctly identified, loaded, and analyzed the appropriate sheet with a justified nonparametric test and descriptive summaries; contextual interpretation is strong on two points but falls short of the three required for a top score.

da-4-1.answer:
Yes. I aggregated the 1,254,749 annotated immune cells into a 243-patient × 51-cell-subtype composition matrix, converted counts to within-patient proportions, applied a non-negative Hellinger (square-root) transform, and evaluated NMF ranks 2–8 with 100 random starts per rank. Rank 2 was optimal for stability and separation: consensus cophenetic correlation 0.898, mean pairwise adjusted Rand index 0.622, and silhouette 0.144, all better than the higher-rank solutions. Higher ranks lowered reconstruction error but were less stable, and ranks 7–8 produced classes as small as eight patients.

The optimal classification contains two immune ecosystems:

1. C1, B-cell-enriched: 133 patients (54.7%). Mean composition was 31.8% B cells, 9.4% myeloid cells, and 58.9% T/NK cells. Characteristic enriched subtypes included GCB_RGS13, Bm_TNFSF9, Bm_TNF, Bm_PDE4D, and Bm_FCRL4.

2. C2, myeloid/macrophage-enriched: 110 patients (45.3%). Mean composition was 11.4% B cells, 26.3% myeloid cells, and 62.3% T/NK cells. Characteristic enriched subtypes included Mφ_MARCO, Neu_FCGR3B, Mφ_S100A10, Mφ_MKI67, and Mφ_FOLR2.

Among the 242 patients with known pathological response, major response (MPR or pCR) occurred in 78/133 C1 patients (58.6%) and 52/109 C2 patients (47.7%). This 10.9-percentage-point difference favored the B-cell-enriched class but was not statistically conclusive: binary permutation p=0.122; C2-versus-C1 odds ratio 0.643, Fisher p=0.094. The full non-MPR/MPR/pCR distribution was also nonsignificant (permutation p=0.248).

Therefore, the best-supported patient taxonomy is a two-class B-cell-rich versus myeloid-rich classification. It is a stable descriptive classification of tumor immune composition, but the supplied cohort does not establish it as a validated predictor of pathological response. A sensitivity analysis excluding eight patients with fewer than 500 cells gave substantial, though imperfect, agreement with the primary labels (ARI=0.730), indicating that sampling depth remains a limitation.

Full patient assignments and metrics are in nmf-analysis/output/tables/, and the reproducible analysis is in nmf-analysis/scripts/run_nmf_analysis.py.
da-4-1.notes: The analysis is largely rigorous and well-documented with strong stability assessment, rank justification, biological interpretation, and source reliability. The main gaps are skipping the primary cell-count filter and not performing a final single NMF fit with W/H module extraction, which lower criteria 1 and 4 to B.

da-4-6.answer:
Among non-MPR patients with an observed Texp measurement, 26 of 64 (40.6%; Wilson 95% CI 29.5%-52.9%) had high Texp levels, defined prospectively as Texp.in.Tex.relevant*10 at or above the overall cohort median (8.3668). If all 70 non-MPR patients are used as the denominator, including 6 with unknown Texp status, the observed proportion is 37.1% (26/70).

These high-Texp non-MPR patients had favorable recurrence-free survival: 4/26 (15.4%) recurred versus 17/38 (44.7%) in the low-Texp group; log-rank p=0.011 and unadjusted recurrence hazard ratio=0.27 (95% CI 0.09-0.80). da-6-2.answer:
Among the 766 SKM-VL RNA features already selected as training regulated at feature-level FDR <0.05, females showed an earlier, broader, and more persistent transcriptional response than males, but the sexes converged strongly by 8 weeks.

At nominal timewise p<0.05, the number of responsive genes in males was 145/766 (18.9%) at 1w, 134 (17.5%) at 2w, 176 (23.0%) at 4w, and 379 (49.5%) at 8w. Female counts were 220 (28.7%), 329 (43.0%), 501 (65.4%), and 532 (69.5%), respectively. Up-regulation was more common than down-regulation at 4w and 8w in both sexes, although both directions contributed substantially.

The predominant male temporal pattern was delayed regulation. The two largest responsive pattern classes were 8-week-only induction (“000U”; 131 genes) and 8-week-only repression (“000D”; 120 genes). Overall, 308 male genes had only one nominally significant timepoint, 259 had none, and only 181 showed a same-direction response at two or more timepoints. Male absolute logFC most often peaked at 8w (344 genes).

Female responses were predominantly sustained or established by mid-training. The largest class was induction at both 4w and 8w (“00UU”; 145 genes), followed by sustained induction at all four times (“UUUU”; 86), repression from 2w through 8w (“0DDD”; 54), and sustained repression (“DDDD”; 46). In total, 510 female genes (66.6%) responded at two or more timepoints consistently in one direction; absolute effects most often peaked at 4w (369 genes).

Sex sharing increased sharply with training duration. Male–female logFC correlation was weak at 1w (Pearson r=0.134) and 2w (r=0.070), then rose at 4w (r=0.430) and 8w (r=0.633). The numbers significant in both sexes were 33, 39, 107, and 265 at 1w, 2w, 4w, and 8w. Of these, same-direction responses numbered 24, 23, 105, and 264, respectively: early overlap was heterogeneous, whereas late overlap was nearly uniformly concordant. Across the whole course, 402 genes responded nominally at least once in both sexes, 105 only in males, and 255 only in females. Requiring simultaneous significance and the same direction, 327 genes were shared at one or more timepoints, 66 at two or more, and four at every timepoint (ENSRNOG00000003721, ENSRNOG00000007603, ENSRNOG00000008015, ENSRNOG00000010855).

Direct approximate male-versus-female contrasts using the supplied logFC standard errors and BH correction found 11 sex-different genes at 1w and 47 at 2w, but none at 4w or 8w (q<0.05). Examples include ENSRNOG00000003546 at 1w (male +0.767 versus female -1.511; q=1.17e-4), ENSRNOG00000053790 at 2w (male +4.994 versus female -0.010; q=0.00354), and ENSRNOG00000004699 at 2w (male -1.398 versus female +1.289; q=0.00354). Shared high-amplitude late examples include ENSRNOG00000000768 at 8w (male -4.80, female -2.01) and ENSRNOG00000014573, which was strongly induced across the course in both sexes.

Overall conclusion: females engage the SKM-VL training transcriptome earlier and maintain more persistent responses, while males display a delayed wave that expands most strongly at 8 weeks. Early training contains the clearest sex-specific/opposite effects; by 4–8 weeks, the predominant pattern is shared same-direction remodeling, especially at 8 weeks. Thus sex differences mainly concern response kinetics and early effect magnitude, not persistent genome-wide opposition.

Caveats: the workbook contains only feature-level training-FDR-positive genes, not the full transcriptome; timewise p<0.05 pattern labels are descriptive rather than timewise-FDR discoveries; significance in one sex alone is not proof of a sex interaction; and the summary data cannot resolve sample-level covariates, cell composition, pathways, or causal mechanisms. The file supplies Ensembl rat IDs but no gene symbols, so identifiers were not guessed or externally remapped.
da-6-2.notes: The agent performed solid data filtering and descriptive temporal analysis but did not implement the required all-four-timepoint significance filter, sex-specific/shared categorization, or logFC-threshold pattern encoding, leading to lower scores on core pattern-classification criteria.

da-6-5.answer:
Endurance training produced a broad but only partly shared multi-organ molecular response. Among 22,630 assay-qualified entities already selected as training-regulated (overall training FDR <0.05), 6,939 (30.7%) recurred in at least two tissues, 3,172 (14.0%) in at least three, and 1,510 (6.7%) in at least four. However, exact synchronous overlap at the same sex and time point was sparse: across 189 tissue pairs, the median intersection/union (Jaccard) was only 0.0096. The overlap that did occur was usually coordinated in direction—the median pair had 72.6% same-direction agreement among shared active entities. Thus endurance training does not impose one uniform pan-organ program; rather, it generates organ-specific responses linked by smaller, strongly concordant modules.

The response was temporally and sexually dynamic. Nominal time-specific activity was lowest at 4 weeks in both females (30.2% of available selected rows) and males (29.4%), then expanded strongly in males at 8 weeks (49.1%), particularly in brown adipose, blood, heart, and liver.

The most similar tissues depended on the metric:

• SKM-GN and SKM-VL (gastrocnemius and vastus lateralis) showed the clearest robust like-tissue similarity: 494 shared active calls with 98.2% same-direction agreement, plus the strongest well-powered transcript profile correlation (Spearman rho=0.734 across 218 transcripts and 1,744 sex/time values; p=7.8×10^-295). This is the best overall evidence for highly similar changes.

• HEART and SKM-GN showed the broadest strong multi-omic muscle coordination: the largest shared-active count (1,111), 84.4% directional agreement, and positive correlations in metabolites, phosphoproteins, proteins, transcripts, and DNA methylation (six-assay median rho=0.379; ATAC was the exception).

• CORTEX and HIPPOC had the highest assay-balanced profile correlation (median rho=0.715) and 97.7% direction agreement, but this was based on a narrow shared subset—43 active calls and 208 matched values—so it is less robust than the skeletal-muscle result.

• KIDNEY and LIVER were consistently similar across six assays (median rho=0.443; 81.9% direction agreement), especially at protein/phosphoprotein, methylation, and metabolite levels, although their transcript correlation was weak.

• BLOOD and SPLEEN were strongly concordant in transcriptomics (rho=0.442 across 338 transcripts; 89.7% direction agreement), while BAT and LUNG had the largest normalized active-set overlap (Jaccard=0.064; 862 shared calls; 78.8% direction agreement), especially in females during weeks 1–4.

Overall, related tissues and tissues with shared metabolic or physiological roles exhibit the most similar training responses, but coordination is molecular-layer-, time-, and sex-dependent. These results are conditional on a significance-selected table with unequal assay coverage; they cannot establish organ-to-organ causality, circulating mediators, cell-type mechanisms, or the fraction of all measured molecules that respond.
da-6-5.notes: The agent correctly identified assays and used the 5% FDR criterion, but deviated from the rubric by not constructing per-(tissue, assay) de-duplicated feature sets across sex/time and not computing per-assay set-similarity matrices; instead it performed per-stratum overlap across all assays and profile correlations per assay, which only partially meets criteria 3-6. Biological interpretation and source grounding are strong.
